articles.abstract: For the last few decades, there has been much debate about a potential bilingual benefit on inhibitory control. To shed light on the debate, we aimed to address both the current methodological and conceptual limitations in the field: (1) the inconsistent use of inhibitory control tasks and measures; and (2) the unexplored role of variability in bilingual experience. Through two studies, the current work aimed to identify tasks and measures with strong psychometric properties to index inhibitory control (Study 1; N = 219). Then, having minimized psychometric concerns, we investigated whether individual differences in bilingual language experience were associated with inhibitory control performance (Study 2; N = 177). In Study 1, multiple task designs and outcome measures were assessed using four commonly used inhibitory control tasks in young adults. Results showed that incongruent/no-go drift rate from a drift diffusion model (DDM) emerged as the most reliable and coherent indicator of inhibitory control. In Study 2, initial analyses indicated that bilingual experience factors (second-language age of acquisition, proficiency, exposure, and linguistic distance) did not jointly predict inhibitory control ability, and no moderating effect of second-language exposure was observed. However, through exploratory analyses, a consistent positive effect of exposure was found in subsamples with sufficient variability in second-language exposure. Taken together, these results suggest that relations between bilingual experience and inhibitory control may be detectable when samples contain sufficient variability in relevant language experience dimensions; future studies should therefore carefully consider both measurement choices and sample characteristics.

articles.title: Spatial proximity differentially modulates goal-directed action and inhibition
articles.authors: Yansong Li; Farzad Rostami; Zixuan Tang; David A. O’Connor; Edmund DERRINGTON; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Goal directed action and inhibitory control are essential for adaptive behavior, yet how these processes are shaped by the spatial proximity of objects remains unclear. Stimuli within peripersonal space may facilitate action while also increasing impulsive responses, suggesting a complex interaction between spatial encoding and cognitive control. Here, we used functional MRI and a three dimensional Go No Go task to examine how apparent physical proximity influences the behavioral and neural correlates of action execution and inhibition. Apparent distance was manipulated using binocular disparity and contextual perspective cues, allowing perceived proximity to be dissociated from retinal size. Behaviorally, participants responded faster and more accurately to near than far stimuli, regardless of apparent or retinal size. At the neural level, both action execution and inhibition recruited a shared cingulo insular control network. Within this network, anterior insula activity was modulated by spatial proximity in a task dependent manner: activity was greater for far than near stimuli during action execution, but greater for near than far stimuli during inhibition. These findings show that peripersonal space differentially shapes action and inhibition through flexible modulation of domain general control networks, rather than relying on separate mechanisms for near and far space.

articles.title: Reimagining Mental Health Through Decolonial Lenses: Protocol for a Qualitative Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis of African Conceptualisations and Responses to Mental Distress and Wellbeing
articles.authors: Daniel Duma Zulu; Drascillar Chilufya
articles.abstract:
Background
Mental distress and wellbeing are understood and experienced through culturally, socially, spiritually, and historically situated worldviews. Yet global mental health research has predominantly been in- formed by conceptual frameworks developed in Euro-American contexts, which may not fully reflect the diversity of African understandings and responses. Although qualitative studies conducted across African contexts have documented culturally grounded understandings of mental distress and wellbeing, this evidence has not been comprehensively synthesised through a decolonial interpretive lens. A qualitative evidence synthesis is therefore needed to consolidate existing knowledge and inform more culturally re- sponsive approaches to global mental health research, policy, and practice across Africa.

Objective
This protocol outlines a qualitative systematic review employing thematic synthesis that aims to synthe- sise qualitative evidence on African conceptualisations of mental distress and wellbeing, culturally grounded responses, and their relationship with dominant biomedical paradigms to generate higher-or- der insights relevant to global mental health.

Methods
The review will follow established guidance for qualitative evidence synthesis, including PRISMA-P, EN- TREQ, PRISMA-S, and the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis. Qualitative studies and mixed-methods studies with extractable qualitative findings conducted in African contexts will be identified through sys- tematic searches of bibliographic databases, grey literature sources, and supplementary search meth- ods. Eligibility will be guided by the SPIDER framework. Methodological quality will be appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) Qualitative Checklist, while confidence in synthesised findings will be assessed using GRADE-CERQual. Findings will be synthesised using Thomas and Harden's thematic synthesis approach and interpreted through a decolonial lens informed by Indigenous knowl- edge systems and critical global mental health scholarship.

Discussion
By centring African epistemologies within qualitative evidence synthesis, this review aims to strengthen the evidence base for culturally responsive and epistemically inclusive approaches to global mental health while informing future research, policy, practice, and social and behaviour change initiatives in Africa and beyond.

articles.title: Psychological Inflexibility in Written Language: Convergent Validity and Associations with Posttraumatic Stress Symptomology and Impairment
articles.authors: Stefphanie M Gambrell; Kapil Chauhan; John Donahue
articles.abstract: Expressive writing, particularly written emotional disclosure (WED), has a range of beneficial outcomes, including reductions in posttraumatic stress (PTS) symptomology, and interventions that employ WED are effective in the treatment of PTSD. Theory and empirical evidence supports the role of psychological inflexibility in the development and maintenance of PTS symptoms, and recent studies have begun to analyze psychological inflexibility in verbal contexts, including WED exercises. The content of WED narratives is a rich source of information in examining underlying theories of PTS symptomology, however this area is virtually unexplored with regard to psychological inflexibility. The present study sought to examine the validity of psychological inflexibility coded in WED narratives in a community sample (N = 415). Results support the convergent validity of coding written psychological inflexibility, as seen by negative associations with self-report psychological flexibility and positive associations with PTS symptoms and anxiety-related distress and impairment. Further, written psychological inflexibility predicts PTS-related outcomes over and above variance explained by self-report psychological flexibility, history of cumulative exposure to potentially traumatic events, and narrative word counts. Findings from the present study extend the small but growing literature on the validity and utility of evaluating features of psychological inflexibility in language.

articles.title: Thinking through metaphor in a second language: A study of whether metaphors benefit the science learning of L2 students compared to literal explanations
articles.authors: Lindsay Krebs; Maddalena Bressler; Luca Bischetti; Laura Baiocco; Cagatay Cora; Valentina Bambini; Vicky Tzuyin Lai
articles.abstract: Metaphors are widely used to teach abstract science concepts, but their effectiveness for students learning in a second language (L2) is unknown. Prior research on metaphoric learning has primarily focused on first language (L1) classrooms, and research on L2 metaphor comprehension has focused on language acquisition or metaphoric competence in L2. We investigated whether metaphorical explanations of science concepts in L2 facilitate learning of those concepts, and how language background and individual visual imagery ability moderate these effects. Students participated in tutoring in L2 and concepts were taught through metaphors and literal explanations. Student judgments of concept concreteness and familiarity, as well as functional knowledge, were assessed in L2 before and after tutoring. While metaphors were effective in teaching science concepts, they were not more effective than literal explanations. Proficiency variables did not moderate this relationship, but visual imagery was positively associated with greater learning gains in the metaphor condition. Metaphorical aptness did not explain any variance in our models. Our results demonstrate that L2 students can use metaphors to successfully learn science concepts, contradicting past claims that metaphors are barriers to understanding, and expanding research into the role of learners’ individual differences.

articles.title: Exploring Human and AI Emotional Support Through Reframing of Negative Situations
articles.authors: Alina Herderich; Joanna Z. Li; Praveen Nair; Anat Perry; Amit Goldenberg
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to LLMs for emotional support and understanding how such AI support differs from humans is crucial for evaluating the consequences of this use. We focused on a highly researched emotion regulation strategy, cognitive reappraisal, a strategy for alleviating negative emotions through reinterpretation. We compared trained humans and GPT-4 in their reappraisal ability with vignettes (Study 1, N = 868) and in real-time interactions (Study 2, N = 386). GPT-4 was consistently rated as more effective, empathic, and novel by objective raters and recipients of the reappraisals. Incentivizing humans increased time spent on the reappraisals but did not close the gap (Study 3, N = 1477). Labeling reappraisals as AI reduced participants' evaluation of their effectiveness, though GPT-4 was still considered more effective (Study 4, N = 496). Language analysis revealed differences in vocabulary associated with quality, suggesting that specific language use is what drives AI superiority.

articles.title: Biased Judge: Recency Effects, Cautious Convictions, and Conservative Updating in GPT-4o’s Legal Decisions
articles.authors: Mengxuan Qiao; Vanessa Cheung; Leya Lisa Hampson; David Lagnado
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly involved in the judicial process. In this paper, we investigate how a common cognitive bias—the overweighting of more recent evidence—among human fact-finders influences GPT-4o's legal judgments. Using three criminal case vignettes, we prompt GPT-4o to judge probabilities of guilt, verdicts, and conditional probabilities of evidence items under two response modes: End-of-Sequence (EoS) and Step-by-Step (SbS), and three system roles: mock juror, legal expert, and advisor. GPT-4o exhibits recency effects under both EoS and SbS (stronger in SbS), especially in its verdicts: it never gives a guilty verdict when defence evidence appears last. Role framing also influences judgments: the advisory framing moderates recency effects and yields the fewest guilty verdicts, while the mock juror framing shows the largest recency effects and highest conviction rates. Compared to Bayesian posteriors computed from the model's own priors and likelihood assessments, GPT-4o systematically under-updates. We contribute a simple, reproducible paradigm for probing order effects in LLMs.

articles.title: In God We Trust, In AI We Ask: Religiosity and Moral Advice Seeking in the AI Age
articles.authors: Helen Huiting Zheng; Kyle Fiore Law; Sara Haman; David DeSteno; Liane Young
articles.abstract: As AI chatbots increasingly enter domains long considered uniquely human, such as moral guidance, questions arise about how they intersect with traditional frameworks like religion. While it is commonly assumed that religious individuals would resist AI intrusion in the moral sphere, we found the opposite. Across two pre-registered studies with a stratified U.S. sample (N=695), both self-reported religious engagement and religious belief were consistently associated with greater openness to seeking moral advice from AI systems. To lay the groundwork for understanding the landscape of psychological factors that may intervene in this relationship, we conducted first-pass parallel mediation analyses using cross-sectional data. These models indicate that the relationship is statistically accounted for primarily by a broader disposition to seek moral guidance from multiple sources, and secondarily by the perceived authority of AI as moral advisors. As we make no causal claims in this study, we invite future experimental work that manipulates these mediators to establish potential causal relationships. Rather than shielding individuals from AI’s appeal in the moral domain, this study indicates that religiosity may systematically facilitate it. These findings carry broad societal implications for AI-mediated moral guidance, a new challenge requiring coordinated attention from technologists, faith communities, and policymakers alike.

articles.title: Presence of Dissociative Experiences in Chronic Illness: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Jeremy Cooper; Courtney E Bowser
articles.abstract: Phenomenological notions of embodiment can coincide or differ from clinical definitions of embodiment. For chronic illness, specifically those in which a sense that one’s life is altered going forward, research has established the need for individuals to have open and flexible mindsets to cope with pain and changes to one’s identity. The question we sought to ask was whether dissociative symptoms manifest in chronic illness presentations, and if so, how these symptoms may present given the possibilities that phenomenology offers for a broader definition of the experience. This systematic literature review followed the PRISMA format, sorting through several of the largest psychological and medical journal databases to identify eight articles that included mentions of dissociative symptoms in those with chronic illness. The full process for this review can be seen throughout this study. The themes we gathered included navigating chronic illness, coping, predisposition, experiential, somatization, and ways of relating. The discussion outlines how dissociative symptoms are not a significant feature to chronic illness, but present in a pre-symptom fashion that can be worsened to a distressing experience dependent on their mindset and coping strategies. Implications for treatment and future research are offered at the end.

articles.title: Perceived authenticity in AI conversational agents: Conceptualizations, operationalizations, and its relationship with anthropomorphism — A scoping review protocol
articles.authors: Maciej Ignatowski; Pawel Strojny
articles.abstract: The objective of this scoping review is to investigate how authenticity is conceptualized and operationalized in research on AI conversational agents and how it is theoretically and empirically related to anthropomorphism. AI conversational agents are increasingly embedded in everyday life, and research has begun to describe user–AI conversational agent interactions using relational constructs such as trust, attachment, and authenticity. Empirical findings indicate that perceived authenticity may influence user engagement and relational outcomes. However, existing studies apply divergent definitions, operationalizations, and research models, particularly regarding the role of anthropomorphism. To date, no comprehensive mapping of these approaches has been conducted. The review will include peer-reviewed theoretical and empirical studies addressing users’ perceptions of authenticity in relation to AI CAs (e.g., chatbots, virtual agents, AI companions). No restrictions will be imposed on participant characteristics or research context. The review will be conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews and reported following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The following databases will be searched: Web of Science, Scopus and PubMed. Two independent reviewers will perform study selection and data extraction. Extracted data will include study characteristics, definitions and operationalizations of authenticity and anthropomorphism, theoretical frameworks, and reported relationships between these constructs. Results will be presented in tabular form and supplemented with a descriptive summary.

articles.title: Self-harm in autistic and non-autistic people: network structure and prediction of suicidality over time
articles.authors: Rachel Moseley; Ido Shalev; Carrie Allison; Simon Baron-Cohen; Nicola Gregory; Victoria Newell; Mirabel Pelton; Tanya L Procyshyn; Elizabeth Weir; Florina Uzefovsky
articles.abstract:
Background
Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is relatively common among autistic people. While studies indicate relationships between NSSI and suicidal thoughts and behaviour (STB), it is unclear whether specific NSSI behaviours co-occur in meaningful ways with differential relevance to STB, and if this differs between autistic and non-autistic people.
Methods
To understand the clinical relevance of specific NSSI behaviours to STB and related constructs, we pooled data from 327 autistic and 260 non-autistic participants from two online surveys. We used network analyses to separately visualise and compare the NSSI networks of autistic and non-autistic people, controlling for age differences between groups. Thereafter, using data provided by autistic people across two time-points one year apart, we examined zero-order correlations and used LASSO regression to assess links between NSSI behaviours at the first time-point and STB-related variables at the second.
Results
Our first analyses revealed differences between autistic and non-autistic people in the co-occurrence of NSSI behaviours and their relationships to STB-related constructs. Three NSSI clusters emerged for autistic people and one for non-autistic people. In both groups, some NSSI behaviours were only indirectly linked to STB via relationships to other NSSI behaviours; cutting and ingesting dangerous substances/sharp objects were most strongly related to suicide attempts. Our second analyses, focusing on autistic people, revealed initial correlations between cutting, self-burning, self-hitting and skin-tearing and STB-related outcomes, although these disappeared after controlling for STB at time-point one. Self-biting, breaking bones and fighting to get hurt remained significant predictors of STB-related outcomes. 
Conclusion
While requiring replication in better matched samples, our findings corroborate differences in how autistic and non-autistic people engage in NSSI, as well as differential relevance of specific behaviours to STB. Future research must explore direct and indirect pathways between NSSI behaviours and STB, and the functional needs that different behaviours serve.

articles.title: A comparison of different measures of slow wave activity across nocturnal ad libitum home sleep in adults
articles.authors: Sareh Panjeh; Tamara P. Taporoski; Kristen Knutson; Hugo Cogo-Moreira; Alexandre da Costa Pereira; Felipe Beijamini; Sabine Pompeia
articles.abstract:
Study objectives: the decline of slow-wave activity (SWA) during sleep, a classic marker of dissipation of homeostatic sleep pressure (DHSP), was assessed very differently among studies of nocturnal sleep in adults, not all of which adjusted for age and sex. It is therefore unclear which is the most reliable way of determining the consistency of these SWA changes and how demographics influence them. 
Methods: SWA (0.5-4 Hz) in N2/N3 sleep stages was assessed over one night’s home polysomnography in a Brazilian community sample (20-59-year-olds; N=427; 237 women). SWA dynamics was analyzed using full mixed-effect models (with random and fixed intercepts and slopes) considering linear and exponential functions of various different SWA metrics [across all available 30 s sleep epochs (whole sample) and mean, peak and total SWA power per NREM sleep cycle in subgroups of participants’ who exhibited four, five and six cycles], before and after adjusting for age, sex and interactions.
Results: of the 30 tested MEMs, only linear per cycle models complied with statistical/modelling assumptions, irrespective of SWA metric, and exhibited the same pattern of effects: SWA decayed (fixed slope effects), but not significantly after adjusting for demographics, which altered both average (fixed) and individual difference (random) effects.
Conclusion: reliable measures of adult nocturnal sleep SWA dynamics in naturalistic conditions were only obtained when modelled linearly per cycle, but consistent SWA decay was not found when demographics were adjusted for. The usefulness of SWA dynamics alone as a measure of DHSP in adulthood must therefore be reappraised.
Keywords: sleep, slow wave sleep, slow wave activity, polysomnography, electroencephalography, age factors, sex factors, statistical models

articles.title: Meditative Development and Psychological Adverse Effects, Challenging, Unpleasant, and Negative Experiences: A Phenomenological Study of Advanced Meditators
articles.authors: Sebastian Ehmann; Terje Sparby; Vanessa Naughton; Andrea Grabovac; Matthew Sacchet
articles.abstract:
Objective: To investigate meditation-related psychological adverse effects, challenging, unpleasant, and negative experiences (MRPAEs) across meditative development and specifically advanced meditation, an emerging domain in contemplative science that remains understudied despite its potential for radically positively transforming, and in some cases destabilizing, mental health.
Design: A qualitative study using semi-structured phenomenological interviews and inductive, content-driven thematic analysis. Theoretical saturation was monitored iteratively, interrater reliability was assessed throughout the coding process, and methodological reporting adhered to the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ).
Participants: 28 advanced meditators with extensive long-term practice histories who were proficient in advanced practices.
Setting: Remote, in-depth interviews conducted with advanced meditators with diverse contemplative backgrounds.
Results: Across 55 interviews, participants described wide-ranging negative and appraisal-dependent experiences spanning affective, cognitive, relational, clinical, and existential domains. Seven major themes were identified: (1) broadly negative cognitive, attentional, and existential disruptions; (2) negative affect, including mood disturbance, anxiety, and fear; (3) adverse impacts on life trajectory and interpersonal relationships; (4) negative clinical and non-clinical transformative experiences, including clinically significant psychiatric symptoms and trauma activation; (5) foundational instability associated with specific meditative insights; (6) ambiguous experiences of context-dependent valence; and (7) resolution strategies, including meditative techniques, teacher guidance, and interpersonal support.
Conclusions: Advanced meditation can precipitate significant psychological challenges across multiple domains. Although meditative development is also associated with profound positive transformation, these findings highlight the importance of distinguishing productive challenge from genuine harm, and provide initial empirical evidence that meditative development warrants dedicated clinical frameworks and interdisciplinary support structures.

articles.title: Performance and biases of the LENA® and ACLEW algorithms in analyzing language environments in Down, Fragile X, Angelman syndromes, and populations at elevated likelihood for autism
articles.authors: Lavechin; Lisa R. Hamrick; Bridgette Kelleher; Amanda Seidl
articles.abstract: Wearable recorders are being used in research and clinical practice to collect and measure children’s vocalizations and language environments. Recordings generate vast amounts of audio, making manual analysis impractical and requiring automated processing. Two automated algorithms have emerged: the proprietary LENA® (Language ENvironment Analysis) and the open-source ACLEW (Analyzing Child Language Experiences around the World) systems; yet, systematic performance comparisons remain scarce. Here, we validate and compare the performance of these two algorithms across key measures: audio segmentation into speaker categories, Conversational Turn Count (CTC), Adult Word Count (AWC), and Child Vocalization Count (CVC). This analysis is based on 25 hours of manually annotated audio recordings from 50 age-matched U.S. children with diverse neurodevelopmental profiles: children with Down, Fragile X, and Angelman syndromes, children at elevated likelihood of autism, and low-risk controls. We hypothesized that the algorithms might be less accurate for children with neurodevelopmental conditions, since these children often show different patterns of volubility and vocal maturity compared to the typically developing children used to train the algorithms. Thus, we assessed the performance of algorithms across diagnostic groups, a crucial validation step for both cross-population research and the evaluation of language interventions. Results reveal that while algorithms achieve similar performance, they show different patterns: LENA® makes fewer segmentation mistakes but misses many segments (identification error rate = 81.3%, percent correct = 45.3%), while ACLEW shows the opposite pattern (identification error rate = 129.4%, percent correct = 69.4%). Both LENA® and ACLEW achieve reasonable levels of accuracy in their automatic counts (Pearson’s r ranging from .78 to .92) and maintain stable performance across diagnostic groups. We conclude with recommendations for the validation and potential use of these algorithms in research and clinical practice.

articles.title: Performance and choice measures in an experimental context reveal strong preferences for self-benefitting compared to pro-environmental outcomes
articles.authors: Sarah Kusch; Ayala Denul; Anne E Urai; Ruth Krebs
articles.abstract: Since spending cognitive effort is costly, individuals have to decide not only how much effort to spend but also for which causes. This depends on the subjective value assigned to the expected outcomes. Typically, this is studied using personal rewards but investing effort is also highly relevant for outcomes that are non-personal, such as pro-environmental ones. Previously, it has been shown that individuals are less willing to invest cognitive effort (indexed implicitly by slower reaction times in a counting Stroop task) to generate pro-environmental than personal rewards. Given the complex relationship between implicit measures and explicit, deliberate choices, it is unclear how implicit performance measures map onto explicit choices whether to spend cognitive effort for environmental causes. To investigate this, we replicated and extended a previous study in a pre-registered online experiment (n = 234). Besides assessing how much effort participants spent on a Stroop task to generate self-benefitting or environmental outcomes, we added trials where participants could explicitly choose for which cause they want to spend effort. Either before or after having spent effort, participants could switch to the respective other outcome. We found that participants chose the self-benefitting outcome much more often (on 79.4% of the switch trials) and improved task performance specifically on trials featuring self-benefitting outcomes. Our data indicate that pro-environmental outcomes have a lower subjective value compared to self-benefitting ones. We discuss these findings in the context of the relationship between implicit and explicit measures of psychological constructs and potential opportunities for behavior change interventions.

articles.title: Encoding models in functional magnetic resonance imaging: the Voxelwise Encoding Model framework
articles.authors: Matteo Visconti di Oleggio Castello; Fatma Deniz; Tom Dupré la Tour; Jack L. Gallant
articles.abstract: One of the major goals of cognitive neuroscience is understanding how the brain represents information about its own internal states and about the external world. This goal can be addressed by creating encoding models that reveal the information represented explicitly in measured brain activity. Here we describe the Voxelwise Encoding Model (VEM) framework for creating encoding models with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. The VEM framework provides several key advantages over traditional neuroimaging approaches. First, the VEM framework is applicable to most experimental designs, from classic factorial designs to complex naturalistic experiments such as movie watching or video games. This flexibility enables researchers to study brain function across multiple domains with the same analytical approach. Second, hypotheses about functional representations are defined and tested quantitatively by extracting feature spaces from experimental stimuli or tasks. These feature spaces quantify specific types of information potentially represented in brain activity and can range from simple human-derived labels to complex features generated by deep neural networks. If a feature space can be used to linearly predict brain activity, the brain is considered to explicitly represent features within that feature space. This prediction approach provides a systematic way to test hypotheses about functional representations. Third, the VEM framework implements robust data science methods to improve model estimation and minimize false positive results. Encoding models are estimated on a training set and validated on an independent test set. Testing in an independent dataset provides direct evidence that experimental findings generalize beyond the dataset used for model estimation. Finally, voxelwise encoding models can be created in each participant's native brain space without unnecessary information loss due to spatial averaging or template resampling required by conventional group analyses. This enables the VEM approach to reveal fine-grained functional organization in individual participants that might otherwise be ignored. In this article, we provide a comprehensive guide to the Voxelwise Encoding Model framework through all phases of research, from experimental design and data collection to the estimation and interpretation of voxelwise encoding models.

articles.title: The Effect of Psychological Distance on Level of Construal: What do we Learn from the CLIMR Failed Replication?
articles.authors: Nira Liberman; Ori Levit-Mor
articles.abstract: Calderon and her colleagues (2026) failed to replicate Constural Level Theory’s (CLT, Liberman & Trope, 2014; Trope & Liberman, 2010) finding that psychologically more distant actions—actions that are planned for the more distant future, for more distant places, for less likely situations and those performed by more socially distant persons- are construed more abstractly. There is considerable evidence for the effect of psychological distance on construal level, including recent, well-powered, preregistered studies. There is also a theory behind this effect: Higher-level constructs change less over distance. So why did the replication fail? What can we learn from it about (studying) distance and level-of-construal, and more generally, about multi-lab replications? This commentary suggests that in several respects, the replication project fell short of meeting established standards of psychological research. The results of the project are partly based on samples that included many inattentive participants, on responders who were not native speakers of the language in which the experiment was presented, on translations that did not preserve the original intent of the materials, on manipulations of distance that were confusing, weak, or confounded with valence and on manipulation-checks that did not check the actual manipulations. The commentary also offers a re-analysis of some of Calderon and colleagues’ (2026) data and a new replication study, both of which show an effect of temporal distance on construal level. Finally, we suggest two ways in which the Registered Replication Report format may be improved.

articles.title: On Bias in Detecting Bias: A Signal Detection Analysis of Attributions to Gender Discrimination
articles.authors: Marie Jakob; Anat Shechter; Jimmy Calanchini; Karl Christoph Klauer
articles.abstract:
Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their group membership, and detecting discrimination is a necessary first step in countering it. Attributions to discrimination have often been conceptualized in terms of Signal Detection Theory (SDT), with researchers speculating about the role of sensitivity (i.e., observers’ ability to recognize discrimination) and response bias (i.e., their tendency to judge that discrimination is present) in observers’ judgments. Here, we take a first step toward moving beyond conceptual applications to empirical SDT analyses of attributions to
discrimination across five studies examining judgments about gender discrimination in corporate pay raise decisions. We find that prototypes (Studies 1 to 3) and their alignment with the actual pattern of decisions (Studies 2 to 4) inform observers’ response bias, reflecting differences in their attribution of unfair outcomes to discrimination (Study 5). In contrast, the extent of harm caused by discriminatory outcomes exerts a small effect on sensitivity and a large effect on response bias (Studies 1 to 3), which reflects observers’ determination of a fair standard for decisions (Study 5). Theoretically, the present work contributes to the causal analysis of central factors shaping attributions to discrimination. Specifically, we shed light on whether effects of these factors are mediated by response bias or sensitivity, and assess their causal origin in either the application of a merit standard or attributional processing.

articles.title: What’s Wrong with Motivated Reasoning?
articles.authors: Armand Bardeau; Bastien Trémolière; David C. Vaidis
articles.abstract: Motivated reasoning is commonly invoked to explain cognitive biases, yet the paradigm faces growing scrutiny. In this article, we synthesize recent conceptual and methodological critiques to argue that these limitations stem from a common root: the progressive dilution of Kunda’s (1990) original distinction between directional and accuracy goals. This conceptual drift has reduced motivated reasoning to mere biased reasoning (Saucier et al., 2025), leading to empirical practices that infer motivational states from outcome biases without directly manipulating or measuring the underlying goals, thereby creating an observational equivalence problem (Druckman & McGrath, 2019; Tappin et al., 2020). Consequently, current methodological refinements fall short of resolving these ambiguities. We argue that valid inference requires explicitly disentangling the nature of the motivation (directional vs. accuracy) from its intensity. To move the field forward, we advocate for a new conceptual framework—integrating Nature and Intensity as orthogonal dimensions—to serve as a theoretical anchor for future research. Such a paradigm would allow reliable discrimination between directional and accuracy goals through converging evidence from behavioral, self-report, and physiological indicators, ultimately re-establishing the theoretical coherence and empirical validity of motivated reasoning research.

articles.title: The Impact of Stress Reappraisal and Mindset Interventions on Physiological, Endocrine, and Psychological Stress Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Karishma K. Singh; Audrey-Ann Journault; Jeremy Jamieson
articles.abstract: How individuals think about stress—their appraisals and beliefs—directly shape stress responses. This meta-analysis assessed the efficacy of psychological interventions aimed at helping people value stress as growth supportive and use it to thrive, referred to as stress optimization interventions, on physiological (cardiovascular and neuroendocrine) and subjective stress-related outcomes. Data from 35 studies (total N = 6,834) that used randomized designs and reported biological or self-reported outcomes before and after stress reappraisal, stress mindsets or a combination of these interventions were analyzed. Random-effect models indicated that stress optimization interventions functioned to increase cardiac output (CO; d = 0.41), decrease total peripheral resistance (TPR; d = 0.47), and reduce salivary cortisol levels (d = 0.20) in acute stress contexts, with small-to-medium effect sizes. These effects were accompanied by small-to-high heterogeneity as a function of outcome (I² from 0% to 67%). No effects of interventions on pre-ejection period (PEP; d = 0.11) or heart rate (HR; d = -0.03) emerged. For subjective outcomes, interventions showed small but reliable benefits. Stress optimization interventions reduced recent distress (d = 0.30) and improved affective responses (d = 0.15), with meaningful heterogeneity across both. In contrast, interventions exhibit no significant effect on reported stress arousal (d = 0.07) with little heterogeneity. Collectively, findings demonstrate that stress optimization interventions can help improve physiological and subjective stress-related responses in acute stress settings, offering a promising approach to promoting resilience, thriving, and performance when navigating everyday social stressors.

articles.title: People make history-dependent decisions in Markovian environments
articles.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Evan Russek; Ionatan Kuperwajs; Nitzan Shahar; Marcelo G Mattar; Wei Ji Ma; Tom Griffiths
articles.abstract: Many real-world decisions are history-dependent, such that the appropriate action depends on recent events. However, people may also encounter history-independent environments, where all information relevant for action selection is contained in the current state. Here, we tested whether people can adapt to such environments by analyzing the behavior of 74,304 online chess players, focusing on 183,775 instances where a player encountered the same board position in two different games. In chess, the configuration of pieces on the board fully specifies the information relevant for optimal play, making the history of the current game redundant. Nevertheless, we find that players’ behavior is biased to be history-dependent. Our findings challenge assumptions about humans’ ability to decide based on a task’s abstract state representation, instead suggesting that contextual traces play a significant role in biasing behavior even when individuals are highly trained and motivated to perform at their best.

articles.title: The Value of Self-Deception: How Conflict in Action Selection May Shape Human Beliefs and Behavior
articles.authors: Boaz Rosenberg; Eran Eldar
articles.abstract:
Human decision-making often involves conflict between different processes involved in guiding behavior. Here we develop a formal account of how self-deception could arise as a byproduct of such conflict. The core idea is that when a process’s preferred action is rejected due to conflict with competing processes, it may still influence choices by promoting attentional biases that shift decisions toward its preferred action. 
We use three proof-of-principle simulations to derive the consequences of this architecture. The simulations show that, under specified conditions, agents can learn to value attentional bias, maintain uncertainty when it makes bias effective, and devalue bias when it is unsustainable. We then outline the qualitative predictions of the model for human behavior, including biased belief formation, self-handicapping, procrastination, and depressive and bipolar-like conditions. We conclude by comparing these predictions with those of existing theories and discussing implications for psychological research and clinical practice. 
This framework offers new theoretical insights into the adaptive and maladaptive functions of self-deception, suggesting it as a key organizing construct for understanding a range of everyday and pathological human behaviors.

articles.title: The Youth-GEMs project: genetic and environmental interactions underlying trajectories of youth mental health
articles.authors: Bart Ruttens; Sinan Guloksuz; Bochao Lin; Covadonga M. Díaz-Caneja; Elisabeth Binder; Jonathan Mill; ESMERALDA RUIZ; Karim Lekadir; Maria Bulgheroni; Jim van Os
articles.abstract: Most mental disorders emerge before age 24, yet the mechanisms shaping youth mental health trajectories remain poorly understood. Here, we present the Youth-GEMs consortium performing a multidisciplinary, multisite research project funded by a European Union Horizon-Staying-Healthy-2021 grant. The Youth-GEMs project (Gene Environment interactions in Mental health trajectorieS of Youth) has an integrated, developmental framework that examines how genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors dynamically interact to influence risk and resilience across adolescence and young adulthood. The project combines developmental (epi)genomic mapping of the human brain, genomic analyses of trans-syndromal phenotypes, exposome-wide environmental assessment, and Artificial Intelligence-based modelling to identify predictive and actionable markers of mental health trajectories of young people. By harmonizing multimodal data from existing population-based cohorts and by establishing the first international, trans-syndromal clinical cohort of help-seeking young people, Youth-GEMs is generating biologically informed polygenic and exposomic scores, cell-type-specific regulatory annotations, and interpretable machine-learning models. Continuous engagement with young people, clinicians, and stakeholders ensures that findings translate into tools for early detection, monitoring, and personalized intervention. Together, these efforts aim to advance mechanistic understandings of youth mental health, improve prediction of emerging illness, and support the development of evidence-based, developmentally sensitive approaches to prevention and care.

articles.title: When ASMR Becomes Unpleasant: Acoustic Features and Visual Context Shape Emotional Responses to Eating Sounds
articles.authors: Daigo Hozaki; Hibiki Okita; Takahiro Ezaki; Hirohito M Kondo
articles.abstract: Autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) videos can evoke both pleasant and unpleasant emotional responses. Eating sounds appear to produce especially large individual differences in these experiences. We examined how acoustic features and visual context shape emotional responses during eating-sound ASMR. Ninety-six participants were randomly assigned to one of four stimulus-presentation conditions: auditory-only (Aud), audiovisual congruent (AV-C), audiovisual incongruent (AV-I), or visual-only (Vis). Participants were presented with eight 30-s ASMR clips (4 min total) and provided continuous ratings of their emotional responses on a 3-point valence scale: unpleasant, neutral, and pleasant. Emotional responses differed across conditions. The Aud condition elicited the most unpleasant ratings. This negative bias was reduced when visual information accompanied the sounds, especially in the AV-C condition. Response-category distributions showed the same pattern. To identify low-level acoustic features associated with moment-to-moment changes in emotional responses, we extracted four acoustic features: amplitude, spectral centroid, spectral bandwidth, and instantaneous roughness. For each feature, we computed across-ear averages and left–right differences. We computed lagged Spearman cross-correlations between acoustic features and emotional responses. In the Aud condition, increases in across-ear average amplitude and roughness were followed by shifts toward more unpleasant responses. Evidence for comparable acoustic–emotion coupling was limited in the AV-C condition. These findings suggest that emotional responses to eating-sound ASMR are shaped by acoustic features and visual context. Congruent visual information may reduce unpleasant responses by clarifying the sound source and changing how eating sounds are interpreted.

articles.title: Falling on Fertile Ground: National Identity Rhetoric Mobilises Those High in National Narcissism
articles.authors: Chiara Zazzarino; Stefan Leach; Aleksandra Cislak; Magdalena Formanowicz; Jan Nikadon; Aleksandra Cichocka
articles.abstract: Politicians frequently talk about national identity and commitment to national interests. We examined whether such rhetoric mobilises supporters by exploring the role of national narcissism—a belief that one’s nation is exceptional and entitled to special treatment. We tested whether national identity rhetoric boosts the audience’s national narcissism or whether it appeals to those already high in national narcissism. In six experiments, conducted in the US and UK (Ntotal = 3,716), we measured reactions to AI-generated political speeches (Studies 1, 3, 4 and 6) and social media posts (Studies 2 and 5). We found that participants high in national narcissism perceived messages promoting national identity as more persuasive and were more willing to share them on social media, compared to messages rejecting national identity (Studies 1 and 2) or neutral ones (Studies 3 and 4). We also found that national narcissism predicted voting for (Studies 1 and 3), and broadly supporting (Studies 4 and 6), leaders who appealed to national identity in their speeches, compared to those who did not. In Study 5, we corroborated our findings by relying on behavioural indices of engagement with social media posts on a mock platform. Similar effects were observed for messages promoting national identification and national narcissism. Furthermore, in Study 6, national narcissism predicted support for leaders promoting (vs. rejecting) national narcissism regardless of their partisan affiliation (as Republican vs. Democrat). Across the six studies, we found no reliable evidence that national identity messages affected participants’ own national sentiments.

articles.title: Gaze semantics: A scoping review of how gaze conveys and constrains meaning in social contexts
articles.authors: Nikol Figalová; Anne Böckler; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: Humans rely heavily on gaze to provide and receive information in social settings. Gaze indicates where another person is attending, but its contribution extends beyond spatial orientation. This scoping review synthesises 352 peer-reviewed articles addressing gaze as a meaningful cue in social situations. The term gaze semantics refers to the systematic ways in which gaze carries, shapes, modifies, or constrains meaning. The evidence suggests that gaze typically does not encode determinate mental content: One gaze pattern can carry different meanings across settings. We organise the empirical literature around four operations of gaze. Gaze orients by directing attention toward something, addresses by making someone socially implicated, qualifies states, traits, and other social cues by modifying how they are interpreted, and coordinates by shaping what becomes relevant next in interaction. These operations can act in parallel and are not tied to specific gaze characteristics. One gaze pattern can perform several operations simultaneously, and each operation can be realised by different gaze patterns. Gaze interpretation is inferential and depends on signal properties, perceptual and interactional availability, multimodal and sequential embedding, social and activity frames, gazer and observer states, and interactional history. We conclude that gaze constrains social interpretation while typically remaining semantically underdetermined.

articles.title: A modifiable tunnel environment to study experience of space (TEnvi)
articles.authors: Mark Wünsche; Mathis Jording; Ralph Weidner; Kai Vogeley
articles.abstract:
Perception of spatial extent depends on multiple sources of information, including geometric and motion-related cues such as perspective and optic flow, as well as oculomotor signals (e.g., vergence), yet experimental control over these factors is often limited. We introduce TEnvi, a stimulus-generation framework that enables systematic manipulation of geometric parameters of a tunnel-like virtual environment under continuous optic flow.
TEnvi allows independent manipulation of tunnel width, height, and depth while maintaining controlled perspective projection, shading gradients, and distance-dependent luminance attenuation. The framework integrates an interactive graphical interface with a reproducible rendering pipeline supporting both real-time preview and batch stimulus export. Camera motion is defined as a function of time, ensuring consistent optic flow across preview and rendered stimuli and preventing cumulative numerical drift.
To demonstrate the utility of the stimulus framework, a behavioural validation experiment was conducted in which participants rated perceived room size while the geometric dimensions of tunnel width, height and depth were manipulated relative to a baseline configuration. Ratings were analysed using a linear mixed-effects model with manipulation type and manipulation level as fixed effects and participant as a random intercept. Manipulations of tunnel width produced graded increases in perceived room size across levels. Manipulations of height produced small shifts relative to baseline but did not differ reliably across levels, while manipulations of tunnel depth showed no detectable influence on perceived room size. These results illustrate how the stimulus framework can isolate the perceptual contribution of geometric parameters and provides plausible data of size perception grounded in tunnel width manipulation.

articles.title: Momentary Cognitive and Self-Regulatory Predictors of Daily Alcohol Use: Intent vs. Inhibition
articles.authors: Jennie Lukoff; Ilse H. van de Groep; Reshmi Marhe; Willem-Paul Brinkman; Ingmar H.A. Franken; Andrew Jones; Joran Jongerling; Danielle Remmerswaal
articles.abstract:
Background. Drinking intentions consistently predict alcohol consumption, but findings for behavioral measures such as inhibitory control are mixed, particularly in earlier stages of use.
Methods. 142 recreational alcohol users (40 males, 102 females; M = 33.30 years, SD = 14.76) completed a four-day EMA study with three daily prompts assessing alcohol use, craving, perceived control, and planned use, directly followed by a mobile Go/No-Go task assessing inhibitory control. Bayesian multilevel models examined whether inhibition errors, planned use, craving, and perceived control predicted drinking at momentary and daily timescales.
Results. Momentary evidence indicated a positive association between planned use and drinking between (β = 0.18, 95% CrI [0.03, 0.31]) and within-persons (β = 0.31, 95% CrI [0.20, 0.42]), while negative within-person effects emerged for craving (β = -0.12, 95% CrI [-0.23, -0.02]) and perceived control (β = -0.41, 95% CrI [-0.52, -0.28]). Daily evidence found that planned use was positively associated with daily drinking (β = 0.84, 95% CrI [0.44, 1.24]), whereas perceived control was negatively associated with drinking (β = -0.78, 95% CrI [-1.21, -0.36]). No credible evidence was found for within-person effects on daily alcohol use.
Conclusions. Findings suggest that alcohol use in recreational drinkers, may be driven by intentions and self-regulatory beliefs, as opposed to momentary or daily lapses with inhibition. A negative within-person association between momentary craving and alcohol use, despite a positive linear study trend, may reflect a mismatch between the reference windows measuring craving (right now) and drinking (night before, last two hours).

articles.title: When ASMR Becomes Unpleasant: Acoustic Features and Visual Context Shape Emotional Responses to Eating Sounds
articles.authors: Daigo Hozaki; Hibiki Okita; Takahiro Ezaki; Hirohito M Kondo
articles.abstract: Autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) videos can evoke both pleasant and unpleasant emotional responses. Eating sounds appear to produce especially large individual differences in these experiences. We examined how acoustic features and visual context shape emotional responses during eating-sound ASMR. Ninety-six participants were randomly assigned to one of four stimulus-presentation conditions: auditory-only (Aud), audiovisual congruent (AV-C), audiovisual incongruent (AV-I), or visual-only (Vis). Participants were presented with eight 30-s ASMR clips (4 min total) and provided continuous ratings of their emotional responses on a 3-point valence scale: unpleasant, neutral, and pleasant. Emotional responses differed across conditions. The Aud condition elicited the most unpleasant ratings. This negative bias was reduced when visual information accompanied the sounds, especially in the AV-C condition. Response-category distributions showed the same pattern. To identify low-level acoustic features associated with moment-to-moment changes in emotional responses, we extracted four acoustic features: amplitude, spectral centroid, spectral bandwidth, and instantaneous roughness. articles.title: Acute effects of competitive exercise context and competitive outcomes on mood responses
articles.authors: Sarah Reddin-Conroy; Carly Wender; Meabh Corr; Eric Magrum; Mika Manninen
articles.abstract:
Acute mood responses to exercise are recognised as important determinants of exercise
adherence, yet the influence of competitive team-game context on these responses remains
underexplored. This study compared acute mood responses between team-game and non-
competitive group exercise while controlling for exercise intensity. A randomised crossover
design was employed with 69 physical education students (age range = 19–30 years; 27
females). Participants completed two 20-minute sessions: an indoor soccer game (TS) and a
video-led group exercise session (GE). Mood was assessed pre- and post-exercise using the
Profile of Mood States–Short Form (POMS–SF), and intensity was measured using Borg’s
Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE). Data were analysed using linear mixed-effects
ANCOVA models. Both conditions produced significant and comparable reductions in Total
Mood Disturbance (TMD). However, the TS condition elicited significantly higher adjusted
post-session vigor compared to GE (Δ = 2.33, 95% CI [0.78, 3.88]), Benjamini-Hochberg
(BH) adjusted p = 0.024, d = 0.52). Within the TS condition, competitive outcome influenced
acute mood responses, with winners displaying less Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) (Δ = -
5.81, 95% CI [-11.24, -0.37], p = 0.037, d = 0.40) and Anger (Δ = -2.53, 95% CI [-4.23, -
0.83], adjusted p = 0.024, d = -0.77) compared to losers. These findings suggest that
psychosocial factors of team games – such as competition and cooperation – can contribute to
enhanced energy beyond the effects of exercise alone. Additionally, the findings imply that
even short recreational team games can lead to different mood responses between losers and
winners.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and Individual Differences: A Perspective of the Differential Psychology, Personality Psychology, and Psychological Assessment Division of the German Psychological Society (DGPs)
articles.authors: Ramona Schoedel; Elisa Altgassen; Mitja D Back; Martje Buss; Markus Bühner; Julian M. Etzel; Benjamin Goecke; Sandra Grinschgl; Eric Grunenberg; Ole Hätscher
articles.abstract: In this paper, we examine artificial intelligence (AI) in the context of studying and measuring individual differences across three current topics: AI as a research tool, the design of human-AI interaction, and AI-assisted assessment. Drawing on selected examples, we illustrate the wide-ranging potentials of AI at the conceptual and methodological level, while also showing that its application raises new (research) questions - for instance regarding human competence in dealing with AI, the “personality” of AI systems, or psychometric standards in the use of AI-assisted assessment procedures. Against this backdrop, we discuss key prerequisites for a sustainable integration of AI into both research in personality psychology and individual differences, including critical validation, transparency, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the systematic consideration of individual differences in the responsible design of the human-AI interface.

articles.title: Revisiting the Interpretation of r and R2: A Comment on Funder & Ozer (2019)
articles.authors: Christian Thurn; Michael Dantlgraber
articles.abstract: The article by Funder and Ozer (2019) emphasizes the important aspect that small correlations can be relevant, both theoretically and practically. However, we contend on two key points: (1) We contend that, when choosing between r and R2 as measures of effect size, R2 remains the superior measure. (2) Furthermore, we argue that despite the justified criticism of traditional, rigid thresholds for interpreting effects, the newly proposed guidelines by Funder & Ozer (2019) carry a risk of overinterpretation by conflating two distinct dimensions: the magnitude of a correlation and the relevance of a correlation.

articles.title: Hallucination or confabulation? A psychological reinterpretation of erroneous outputs in large language models
articles.authors: Ignacio Rivero Covelo; Aryan H. Patel; Kaelan J. McDonough
articles.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent but false outputs that are widely described as “hallucinations.” We argue that this term is psychologically imprecise. In clinical psychology and psychiatry, hallucinations are perceptual phenomena, whereas many erroneous LLM outputs are better characterized as constructive, plausibility-guided responses produced under insufficient informational constraint. We suggest that confabulation provides the more informative psychological analogue.

Drawing on work in psychopathology, memory, source monitoring, and natural language generation, we compare hallucinations, confabulations, and LLM errors as distinct classes of cognitive failure. Our central claim is that many LLM errors resemble confabulation more closely than hallucination because they involve coherent but false content generation rather than perception-like experience. This reframing revises terminology. Additionally, it clarifies the kind of process involved and connects AI discourse to established psychological theory. Finally, it generates testable predictions: such errors should increase under ambiguity, decrease with stronger external constraint, and remain schema-consistent rather than random. More broadly, the paper illustrates how psychological concepts can be used productively in interpreting artificial systems, while also showing the importance of distinguishing among superficially similar forms of error.

articles.title: How Will I Know If You Really Like Me? Assessing the Role of Appearance, Behavior, and Reciprocity for Meta-Liking Accuracy in Initial Social Encounters
articles.authors: Jana Bruns; Eva Bleckmann; Lisa Maria Niemeyer; Mitja D Back; Steffen Nestler
articles.abstract: In first social encounters, people regularly try to figure out whether others like them. When accurate, these meta-liking judgments enable individuals to more optimally engage in social interactions. Although previous research shows that people do know how much others like them, little is known about the processes leading to accurate meta-liking judgments. In the present, pre-registered research, we aimed to close this gap by investigating the role of a meta-perceiver’s appearance and behavior, others’ behavior towards that meta-perceiver, and the reciprocity heuristic in forming accurate meta-liking judgments. To this end, we used data from a round-robin study, in which N = 144 participants (Mage = 22.91, 67.6% female) took part in two group meetings, where they interacted with unacquainted others. After each participant had given a short self-introduction, participants indicated liking and meta-liking for each other participant. Additionally, trained raters judged participants’ appearance and behavior during the self-introduction. Results showed that people were able to correctly infer how much others generally liked them but hardly knew how much specific other liked them. Lens model analyses revealed that although one’s appearance and behavior were valid cues for being generally liked, meta-perceivers did not utilize most of these observable cues to inform their meta-liking judgments. However, the assumed reciprocity mediated both individual and dyadic meta-liking accuracy. In light of these findings, we discuss the role of self-observed behavior and stable personality characteristics as well as situational and motivational factors, presenting an integrative theoretical framework to explain generalized and dyadic meta-liking accuracy.

articles.title: The format of metaphorical meaning: Neurophysiological evidence for dynamic and flexible image-based representations
articles.authors: Federico Frau; Rosario Tomasello; Maddalena Bressler; Chiara Pompei; Fabrizio Luciani; Paolo Canal; Valentina Bambini
articles.abstract: Theories of metaphor comprehension have long debated the representational format of metaphorical meaning. While classical accounts describe metaphors as abstract propositional representations, other theories have, to varying degrees, argued that metaphor evokes mental imagery. Yet neurophysiological evidence that speakers construct mental images reflecting the complete figurative interpretation remains scarce. Here, we investigated whether metaphors give rise to mental images resembling those generated during imagery or whether they rely predominantly on propositional representations. We designed a novel picture-matching paradigm in which identical target pictures were preceded by either matching or mismatching stimuli across four tasks: another picture (Physical task), an adjective prompting imagery (Imagery task), a literal sentence (Literal task), or a metaphorical sentence (Metaphorical task). Across multiple levels of analysis of the EEG signal, the Metaphorical task patterned more closely with imagery than with literal language. Metaphors elicited enhanced P300 and attenuated N200 responses, greater recruitment of occipito-temporal visual regions, and stronger upper-alpha/lower-beta desynchronization than literal descriptions, indicating that participants constructed perceptually richer representations. These effects were further modulated by individual differences in imagery and vocabulary. However, at later stages, metaphors also diverged from imagery, which showed more pronounced brain signatures associated with memory retrieval and representational maintenance. These findings indicate that metaphorical meanings yield image-based representations while remaining constrained by propositional content. Collectively, the results confirm that metaphor “sets things before the eyes”, but it does so through the dynamic and flexible interaction of perceptual simulation with propositional information, in line with multiple representation theories of conceptual knowledge.

articles.title: Deviations in Distributions Perception through Imprecision and Accounting for Uncertainty through Abstract Representations
articles.authors: Nico Gradwohl; Benjamin Scheibehenne
articles.abstract: Perceiving the distributions of values we experience accurately is crucial for adaptive judgment and decision making. Previous research shows that people are quite adept at learning distribution information, so that many models of judgment and decision making assume that people accurately store it. However, a variety of deviations in distributions people report indicate that distributions are unlikely stored faithfully, even if the observed information is unbiased. To shed light on the origin of these deviations we review of literature on distribution perception and the cognitive processes underlying the encoding of numeric information. Based on this review, we outline a framework of three cognitive processing steps: perception and encoding, representation formation, and retrieval. Computational descriptions of these steps illustrate that deviations in previous work may originate from imprecise perception, retrieval, as well as integration into abstract representations that account for uncertainty. Based on predictions from the framework, we provide empirical results supporting that both imprecise perception and memory, as well as formation and storage of abstract representations contribute to deviations in the perception of distributions. Results also show that people unlikely just store information as precise instances that are retrieved to make judgments about distributions. This work contributes by connecting previously disconnected literature strands. It also shows that biases in judgments and decisions may not only be the result of biased processing of accurately stored distributions, but also of fundamental distortions in how values and their distributions are perceived.

articles.title: From Review to Synthesis: A Step-by-Step Methodological Guide to Systematic Reviews and Multilevel Meta- Analyses
articles.authors: Hu Meilan; Paye Shin Koh; Xun Ci Soh; Andree Hartanto; Nadyanna M. Majeed
articles.abstract: We provide a step-by-step guide on conducting a quantitative systematic review (i.e., meta-analysis) using the open-source programming language R, as well as conducting a multilevel meta-analysis, in contexts where effect sizes are non-independent (e.g., multiple effect studies from the same lab). Quantitative systematic reviews offer researchers a method to synthesise large bodies of literature, helping to clarify inconsistent findings, identify research gaps, and refine theoretical models. However, existing tutorials often assume prior knowledge and/or experience, often overlooking foundational concepts. To address this gap, a comprehensive walkthrough of the systematic review process is presented, covering pre-registration, literature search and retrieval, screening, risk of bias assessment, and data extraction following the PRISMA framework. We then present detailed guidance on how to conduct both traditional and multilevel meta-analyses in R. Specifically, the tutorial explains how to estimate overall meta-analytic effect sizes when effect sizes are independent (traditional meta-analysis) and when effect sizes are nested within labs (multilevel meta-analysis). Procedures for assessing heterogeneity, testing for publication bias, and conducting moderation analyses are also covered. To accompany this tutorial, we supplement annotated R scripts and R notebooks to support transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility for researchers of all levels of experience.

articles.title: From Pathogens to Paintings: A Preliminary Investigation Into the Behavioral Immune System’s Influence on Visual Aesthetic Appreciation and Perception
articles.authors: Serkan Ozcakan; Mert Tekozel
articles.abstract:
As an antipathogenic psychological adaptation, the behavioral immune system has been associated with a broad spectrum of psychological phenomena, including mating, conformity, xenophobia, religiosity, social prejudice, and food preferences. Additionally, this system may influence artistic appreciation and perception. Activation of the behavioral immune system generally results in intolerance of morphological deviations, even toward stimuli that do not pose a real pathogen threat, as it operates on the “smoke detector principle.” Therefore, we hypothesized that participants exposed to pathogen threats would exhibit less appreciation for abstract paintings—those deviating significantly from figural reality—compared to those under other threats or nonthreat conditions. Supporting our hypotheses, participants under pathogen threat liked abstract and ambiguous paintings (those lying between realistic and abstract) less compared to those in the other two conditions. However, the prediction that ambiguous paintings would be perceived as more abstract under pathogen threat did not receive statistically significant support. These preliminary results suggest that psychology evolved in response to pathogen threats may also influence visual aesthetic appreciation.

Keywords: behavioral immune system, visual aesthetic liking, pathogen salience, art preferences, experimental aesthetic.

articles.title: The effectiveness of a therapeutically applied Dungeons and Dragons group intervention in a community mental health setting – Protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
articles.authors: Terry Rae; Matthew Modini; Poppy Watson
articles.abstract:
Objective 
The use of Therapeutically Applied Role-Playing Games (TA-RPGs) in mental health treatment settings has grown in popularity and early efficacy investigations appear promising. However, the use of TA-RPGs for the treatment of anxiety and depression has rarely been studied in people who present with comorbid complex mental health issues. While one recent waitlist-controlled trial has reported that a TA-RPG (Dungeons and Dragons with embedded CBT) reduced mental health symptomatology, this now needs to be replicated with a more robust experimental design. Publishing this protocol methodology before the study is completed aims to increase transparency and aid other researchers conducting similar research in this advancing field.  
Methods 
The authors propose a two-group randomised controlled trial testing the efficacy of a CBT-infused, therapeutically applied, 8-week Dungeons and Dragons group program. An active control group will play board games for a comparable amount of time. Participants will be consumers receiving care at a community mental health centre with complex care needs. Outcome measures for anxiety and depressive symptomatology will be collected before and after participation in both groups, with the intervention group also completing outcome measures at 12 months follow up. In this protocol paper the intervention will be outlined in detail. The trial is registered on the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12625000296437.

articles.title: A network approach to examining alcohol use and AUD risk factors across adolescence and adulthood
articles.authors: Karis Colyer-Patel; Emese Kroon; Christophe Romein; ajay handa; Janna Cousijn
articles.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) involves a complex interplay of risk factors that are rarely studied in combination, despite likely influencing one another in shaping vulnerability to problematic use. Network analysis offers a means of capturing these interconnections simultaneously, providing insights that traditional analytical approaches cannot. The present study applied this approach to examine (1) the item-level structure of the AUDIT, one of the most widely used screening tools for hazardous alcohol use, and (2) the interconnections among established AUD risk factors, including age of onset, craving, drinking motives, mental health symptoms, impulsivity, and tobacco use (n = 933), comparing networks between adolescents (16-25 years; n = 421) and adults (35-65 years; n = 252). In the AUDIT network, consumption measures clustered strongly together, with binge drinking central in connecting consumption to use-related problems including loss of control. This structure was consistent across age groups, with no differences in network structure or edges. In the AUD risk factor network, alcohol consumption was highly central, drinking motives were strongly interconnected, and mental health symptoms were associated with executive functioning. This structure was again found to be consistent across age groups. However, adolescents reported significantly higher levels of alcohol use, use-related problems, and several AUD risk factors compared to adults. These findings suggest that while the severity of alcohol use, use-related problems and AUD risk factors may differ across development, the underlying relational structure appears comparable.

articles.title: Diffusion MRI of Gray Matter Microstructural Profiles in Healthy Aging
articles.authors: Jenna Louise Merenstein
articles.abstract: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is a non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) acquisition technique that can provide detailed information about brain microstructure. This methodology has historically been applied only to white matter tissue in the research context, but more recent literature suggests that diffusion MRI can also be applied to study microstructural alterations of gray matter tissue, including in healthy aging. The current narrative review evaluates diffusion MRI studies investigating age-related differences in gray matter microstructure and their implications for understanding cognitive function in healthy older adults. The studies reviewed here report widespread age-related differences in cortical (especially frontoparietal), hippocampal, and subcortical microstructure that is behaviorally relevant– especially for cognitive domains of learning and memory. Gray matter microstructure is consistently influenced by the presence of dementia-related pathology, physical activity, and sleep health, but additional research work is needed to understand the roles of biological sex, environment, and dietary intake. Future work of gray matter microstructural profiles in healthy aging should consider longitudinal designs, combining different diffusion MRI modeling techniques in the same study, and defining more specific cognitive correlates (e.g., processing speed).

articles.title: Frequency-dependent selection in the English spelling system across 1000 years of history
articles.authors: Jon W Carr; Kathleen Rastle
articles.abstract: English orthography has largely been left to evolve freely across its thousand-year history with little top-down design or reform. Yet modern English spelling has become standardized, even if its standardized spellings are sometimes internally inconsistent. The relative freedom with which English orthography has been allowed to evolve makes it an interesting test-case for exploring whether spelling standardization might arise through a process of positive frequency-dependent selection. To maximize the chance of being understood, it pays for a writer to adopt spelling variants that occur with higher frequency, leading to those forms becoming increasingly entrenched. To evaluate this possibility, we assembled a diachronic dataset of English spelling variation, SpellEng, which we make freely available. SpellEng reports on the frequency of 112,080 spelling variants (across 32,264 lemmata) over the entire history of written English. We use this dataset along with a model of frequency-dependent selection to estimate the extent to which English standardization can be explained by such a process. Our findings suggest that the past 1000 years of English spelling have been characterized by both positive and negative frequency-dependent selection. We discuss how linguistic dynamics and external events have shaped these periods of stability and change.

articles.title: Mechanistic Explanations Aren’t Immune to Biased or Heuristic Processing
articles.authors: Asheley R. Landrum; Joanna K. Huxster; Ch'Ree Essary; Matthew H. Slater
articles.abstract: Mechanistic explanations have been proposed as a way to reduce public ideological resistance to politicized scientific issues by directing audiences' attention to the causal processes underlying scientific phenomena. In an online experiment, 507 U.S. participants viewed coherent or incoherent mechanistic explanations about climate change or mask-wearing, evaluated the strength of those arguments, and completed a thought-listing task. We assessed objective, systematic processing using three indicators: (1) differentiating between coherent and incoherent explanations in argument-strength evaluations, (2) identifying logical flaws in the incoherent condition, and (3) focusing thoughts on the explanatory mechanism. Participants generally failed to distinguish between coherent and incoherent explanations, only 5% identified flaws, and just 14% produced mechanism-focused thoughts. Instead, most participants exhibited identity-signaling, heuristic, or otherwise non-mechanistic responses, suggesting that mechanistic explanations do not reliably elicit the objective, systematic processing often assumed to underlie their effectiveness.

articles.title: Strategy Over Source: How AI Disclosure Shapes Perceptions of Counterspeech
articles.authors: Yidi Zhang
articles.abstract: As counterspeech is increasingly generated or assisted by artificial intelligence (AI), how its disclosed source shapes audience responses remains unclear. This study examined whether labeling counterspeech as AI-generated, human-written, or unlabeled affects bystanders' evaluations of message strategy and their willingness to post counterspeech against online hate. Using a 3 (source label) × 2 (strategy: empathy vs. humor) × 2 (actual authorship: AI vs. Human) mixed design, 206 participants evaluated counterspeech messages. Disclosing an AI source had no significant effect on perceived strategy implementation or willingness to post, indicating that AI labeling did not penalize messages. In contrast, message strategy mattered: empathy-based counterspeech elicited greater willingness to post than humor-based counterspeech. The qualities of the messages themselves, rather than the labels attached to them, drove participants' responses. These findings suggest that message strategies, more than source disclosure, shape bystander engagement, with implications for the responsible deployment of AI-assisted counterspeech.

articles.title: Firearm Carrying and Purchase Intentions in Permitless Carry States: State Policy or State Culture?
articles.authors: Paul E Teas; Tannuja Rozario; Alexandra Filindra
articles.abstract:
Background. Over the past decade, 29 US states have adopted permitless carry laws, eliminating the requirement to obtain a permit before carrying a firearm in public. Prior research links these policy changes to increases in firearm violence, but less is known about how they relate to individual-level firearm behaviors and purchasing intentions.
Methods. Using a nationally representative cross-sectional survey of firearm-owning and non-owning US adults conducted in the United States in 2024–2025 (N = 18,251), we examined associations between state permitless carry laws and firearm ownership, carrying behavior, carry frequency, purchase intentions, and firearm type.
