articles.abstract: Heterogeneity has been proposed as a framework to improve psychological and behavioral science by identifying mechanisms that explain the differences between replications of an effect. The modal response to such differences is to search for relevant moderators—typically with limited success. We argue that monotonic non-linear relationships can generate heterogeneous effects across replications when baseline levels differ, even in the absence of moderators. To evaluate this possibility, we introduce four descriptors of heterogeneity: effect heterogeneity, control group heterogeneity, the intercept–slope correlation, and the rank correlation between control and treatment means. These characterize patterns consistent with linear, concave, or convex functional relationships. We apply this analytical framework to an initial pool of 55 meta-analytic multi-lab data sets. All data sets with heterogeneous effects also demonstrated control group heterogeneity, and several patterns were in line with a concave functional relationship. In some cases, the association between baselines and effects accounted for a substantial proportion of effect heterogeneity. Additionally, only a small number of data sets were directly at odds with a monotonic non-linear functional form. Moreover, our results suggest that effect heterogeneity in multi-lab research reflects diverse data patterns rather than providing support for treating moderators as the modal explanation for effect heterogeneity. We discuss implications for multi-lab and meta-analytic practice, study design, and interpretations of effect heterogeneity. We advocate for a shift from treating only the effect size distribution as the explanandum of the heterogeneity framework to more elaborate descriptions of heterogeneity.

articles.title: Principled Default Priors for Bayesian Hypothesis Testing in Binomial GLMs:   A Matched-Prior Framework with Empirical Evaluation
articles.authors: Gidon T. Frischkorn; Joscha Dutli; Philipp Musfeld; Klaus Oberauer
articles.abstract: Researchers using Bayesian hypothesis testing in binomial generalized linear models (GLMs; for instance, logistic regression for accuracy data) need priors on regression coefficients, but no widely adopted default framework exists. The nonlinear link function creates a prior-link interaction: priors that appear reasonable on the coefficient scale can imply implausible distributions on the probability scale. We show that this problem has an exact solution for CDF-based link functions: matched priors – prior families whose CDF mirrors the link function – produce uniform distributions on the probability scale for the intercept, a maximally uninformative anchor. We extend this family choice to effect priors for parsimony, with prior scale determined via prior predictive simulation. We embed this matched-prior principle in a three-step workflow and evaluate it via simulation: (1) identify matched priors, (2) evaluate prior predictive distributions, (3) calibrate Bayes factors and compare to the JZS/Cauchy default. For logistic regression, the matched Logistic(0, 0.75) intercept prior and matched Logistic effect priors with scale 0.25 to 0.30 provide well-calibrated Bayes factors. A signal detection analysis shows that prior scale is a criterion parameter: it shifts the operating point on the ROC curve but does not change discriminability. The advantage of the matched-prior workflow is principled scale selection on the probability scale, where effect sizes are directly interpretable. The workflow extends naturally to hierarchical models, where the prior on the random-effects variance has negligible influence on Bayes factors for fixed effects. Ready-to-use brms code and scaling formulas for any contrast coding are provided.

articles.title: Different post-pandemic patterns in youth mental health and wellbeing after a global stressor: variation across domains and informants
articles.authors: Lianne P. de Vries; Hedy van Oers; Cyrina Brouwer; Michiel A.J. Luijten; Jana Runze; Lorynn Teela; Marlene Werner; Josjan Zijlmans; Maaike Oosterling; Hilgo Bruining
articles.abstract:
Objective. The COVID-19 pandemic was a major global stressor for children and adolescents, raising concerns about longer-term consequences for mental health and wellbeing. Many studies reported increased mental health problems during and shortly after the pandemic, but less is known about longer-term post-pandemic patterns across domains and informants.
Method. We used repeated cross-sectional data from Dutch children and adolescents aged 8-18 years in the Netherlands Twin Register (NTR, N = 39,178, 50% girls) and a representative general-population sample (N = 2,782, 48% girls). Parent- and child-reported mental health problems and wellbeing were assessed using pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic data through 2025. Post-pandemic patterns were examined by comparing 2024/2025 outcomes with 2023 and pre-pandemic levels using pre-registered multilevel models.
Results. Parent-reported internalizing and externalizing problems in 2024/2025 did not differ from 2023 levels (B = -0.03 to 0.03), but remained higher than pre-pandemic levels (B = 0.28 to 0.31). Child-reported depressive symptoms were lower in 2025 than in 2023 (B =-2.31), anxiety did not differ (B =-0.75), and anger was higher (B =1.13). Compared with pre-pandemic levels, child-reported depression, anxiety, and anger were all higher in 2025 (p <.001). Wellbeing patterns were mixed across informants and samples (B =-1.05 to 0.10).
Conclusions. Up to 2025, youth mental health and wellbeing did not show a general return to pre-pandemic levels. Patterns differed across domains and informants, highlighting the importance of continued multi-informant monitoring.

articles.title: Infants Use Physical Size, but Not Prior Possession, to Predict Conflict Outcomes, and Do Not Prefer Prior Possessors over Contenders
articles.authors: Erik Kjos Fonn; Joakim Haugane Zahl; Bjørn Dahl Kristensen; Oliver Scott Curry; Lotte Thomsen
articles.abstract: Ownership is a pervasive feature of human social life, yet its developmental origins remain unknown. One influential proposal is that human ownership psychology is built on an early-developing and evolutionary ancient sensitivity to first possession: Across species, conflicts over resources are often settled in favor of whoever held a resource first. Among humans, individuals who take what others already possess are often devalued as cooperative partners. Here, we focused on the inferences and preferences infants and toddlers form based on first possession. Across six laboratory experiments (N = 227), we found positive Bayesian evidence that 10–18-month-old infants and young toddlers do not expect intruders will defer to first possessors in territorial conflict, and that 10–13-month-old infants do not prefer prior possessors over those who take (or attempt to take) possessions from others by force. In contrast, we found that infants do expect that larger, more physically formidable agents will prevail in territorial conflict, using identical methods. Hence, prior possession alone is not sufficient for shaping infants' expectations and evaluations in dyadic conflict, though physical formidability is.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Reliance on Generative AI in Schoolwork: The Role of Executive Functioning Difficulties, Perceived Usefulness, and Habitual Use
articles.authors: Johan Klarin; Eva Hoff; Daiva Daukantaite
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are becoming an increasingly common part of adolescents’ everyday and academic life, raising important questions about which individuals may be more likely to rely on them when facing challenges. Drawing on theories of technology adoption, habit formation, and self-regulation, the present study examined a sequential mediation model linking executive functioning (EF) difficulties to reliance on GenAI, defined as a tendency to depend on GenAI rather than one’s own effort or teacher support when encountering academic challenges, through perceived usefulness and habitual use. The model was tested using structural equation modeling in community samples of lower secondary school students (N = 849, Mage = 14.8 years, 49.4% girls) and upper secondary school students (N = 898, Mage = 17.4 years, 55.2% girls). Across both groups, EF difficulties were positively associated with perceived usefulness, habitual use, and reliance on GenAI (rs = .14–.32, ps < .001). Supporting the hypothesized model, the sequential indirect pathway through perceived usefulness and habitual use was significant in both groups (βs = .08–.10, ps < .001). Perceived usefulness emerged as the most consistent mediator, whereas habitual use showed a more limited mediating role despite being strongly associated with reliance (βs = .60–.69, ps < .001). The findings identify EF as an important individual-difference correlate of reliance on GenAI and suggest that perceived usefulness may be a key mechanism linking EF difficulties to reliance. More broadly, the results highlight the role of self-regulatory capacities in adolescents’ reliance on GenAI.

articles.title: Intertwining experience and evidence: how can co-created causal diagrams guide meaningful research questions about psychosocial processes in pain? A participatory co-design study
articles.authors: Rebecca M. Pearson; Amanda Ly; Neil Heydon-Dumbleton; Alexandria Andrayas; Megan Anne Chambers; Noureen Shivji; Rachael Gooberman-Hill; Samantha Stone; Matthew Nunes; Laura Oporto Lisboa
articles.abstract:
Objectives: To develop and implement a co-creation process for common language and multi-stakeholder engagement to produce a shared causal framework that helps identify meaningful research questions in the context of psychosocial processes in pain and guide data modelling decisions.
Design: Participatory co-design study using facilitated workshops and iterative synthesis to develop a ‘Dream’ Directed Acyclic Graph (Dream-DAG). The Dream-DAG represented an idealised visual causal map unconstrained by available study measures or specific dataset limitations. We used a storm metaphor where different components of the storm (i.e., thunder or lightning) mirror the temporal and causal inference features in DAGs (i.e., exposure or confounding).
Setting: A UK-based multidisciplinary pain research consortium involving researchers, clinicians and public contributors.
Participants: 12 participants took part, including 4 experts by experience living with chronic pain and 8 professionals including a wide range of researchers (from quantitative and qualitative fields), clinicians and data scientists. Participants were invited because of their lived, clinical, methodological or data-related expertise relevant to psychosocial processes in pain.
Results: Through the workshops we developed a shared language for causal thinking, a co-created Dream-DAG, and an operationalised set of hypothesised pathways to inform future data modelling within pain research. The variables and pathways of interest identified as part of this process cover a wide range of concepts considered relevant to the development and maintenance of pain. This included individual factors such as anxiety and loss of identity, interpersonal factors such as disruption to relationships, and the broader role of social worlds. Importantly, the DAG mapped the order of influences and highlighted disruption to relationships as a potential mediating indirect pathway between pain-related experiences and ongoing pain impact. The process also supported translation of experiential, clinical and methodological knowledge into testable research questions for use within existing life-course datasets.
Conclusion: Collaboration using metaphor-based causal diagram development can support multidisciplinary pain research teams to integrate expertise from multiple viewpoints which is vital to ensure that research questions are meaningful to those with chronic pain. The resulting Dream-DAG provides a transparent, theory-informed and experience-informed framework for future empirical analyses, with operationalised and testable hypothesised pathways, although further work is needed to evaluate its transferability to other research teams, datasets and health contexts.

articles.title: Shared and Distinct Structural Features of Autism-Spectrum Traits and Personality Pathology: A Dimensional Approach
articles.authors: Ludwig Ohse; Emanuel Jauk; Kerrin Riedel; Caroline Ibe; Alexander Lischke
articles.abstract: Current evidence suggests overlap between autism-spectrum traits and personality pathology. However, previous studies have mostly relied on categorical models, whereas dimensional approaches are increasingly emphasized in contemporary frameworks of psychopathology. The current study examined shared and distinct structural features of autism-spectrum traits, pathological personality traits, and borderline personality traits in a non-clinical sample of 704 adults. Participants completed self-report measures of these constructs. We estimated confirmatory and exploratory factor models, including bifactor models, to distinguish general from specific personality pathology. Autism-spectrum traits were substantially associated with pathological and borderline personality traits, although associations differed across autism-spectrum trait domains. The communication and reciprocity domain showed the strongest associations across personality pathology domains, followed by social interaction and spontaneity, while the imagination and creativity domain showed rather modest associations. Confirmatory bifactor models indicated that autism-spectrum traits were mainly associated with general personality pathology. After accounting for general personality pathology, detachment was the only specific personality pathology domain that remained substantially associated with autism-spectrum traits, particularly social interaction and spontaneity. Exploratory models largely confirmed these findings. Results suggest that autism-spectrum traits related to social communication and interaction overlap mainly with general personality pathology but also with detachment as a specific personality pathology domain.

articles.title: The Link Between Parental Education and Teenagers’ School Grades is Largely Genetic – Evidence from a Children-of-Twins Study
articles.authors: Josefina Benita Bernardo; Hans Fredrik Sunde; Fartein Ask Torvik; Elsje van Bergen
articles.abstract: Why do children of more highly educated parents obtain better school grades? We addressed whether this reflects environmental effects of parents or familial factors shared across generations, using Norwegian population-register data (1.6 million individuals from 200k extended families) and genetically informative family designs. At age 16, teacher evaluations and national written exams in Norwegian (L1), English (L2), and mathematics were highly similar, with strong phenotypic correlations (r = .68-.84) and near-unit genetic correlations (r = .87-1.00). Associations between parental educational attainment and offspring grades were comparable across teacher evaluations, national exams, and grade point averages (r = .28-.36). For grade point averages, children-of-twins-and-siblings modelling indicated that most parent-offspring resemblance reflected genetic transmission (66%), alongside significant contributions from extended-family (25%) and parental transmission (10%). These findings suggest that intergenerational stability of education largely reflects genetic and extended-family transmission rather than teacher bias or direct effects of parental education alone.

articles.title: New Mothers and Fathers Show Distinct Emotion Dynamics across Maternity and Paternity leave
articles.authors: Christopher Martin Mikkelsen Cox; niels vaerbak; Pernille Højlund Brams; Christine Elizabeth Parsons
articles.abstract: How do first-time parents regulate their own and each other’s emotions as they navigate maternity and paternity leave? Using experience sampling, we tracked Danish mothers and fathers’ emotion states six times daily for a week across maternity (N = 88) and paternity leave (N = 56). Bayesian multilevel coupled-oscillator models revealed distinct emotion regulation patterns that varied systematically with leave arrangements. Arousal amplified self-regulation dynamics specifically for parents not on leave, while co-located partners (verified through GPS) displayed emotional synchrony in both valence and arousal that disappeared in randomly paired couples. Mothers’ regulatory responses to fathers shifted across leave periods, weakly following fathers’ emotions during maternity leave but counterbalancing them during paternity leave, whereas fathers provided weak counterbalancing responses across both periods. These findings, combined with substantial couple-level variation, establish that couples function as mutually regulating systems where individual capacity and leave configurations jointly shape how first-time parents coordinate their emotional lives.

articles.title: Against the Rejection of Large Language Models in Qualitative Research
articles.authors: Evgeny Smirnov
articles.abstract: In 2025, 419 qualitative researchers from 32 countries signed an open letter in "Qualitative Inquiry" rejecting generative AI in reflexive qualitative research. This manuscript offers a critical commentary on these arguments. I review 27 concerns across five domains (technical, methodological, ethical and political, epistemological, and ontological) and argue that many objections (1) target earlier-generation tools, (2) identify challenges LLMs can help mitigate, (3) reflect improper use rather than principled limitations, (4) rely on unresolved philosophical distinctions, or (5) underestimate the inevitability of these tools. This analysis aims to stimulate constructive dialogue rather than rejection.

articles.title: How ball juggling training affects executive function, across the lifespan: Narrative review
articles.authors: Javier Fernández-Ortega; Andrés B. Fernández-Revelles
articles.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Background:
Juggling is a complex coordinative skill integrating visuospatial processing, prediction, bimanual control, and continuous performance monitoring. These characteristics make it a theoretically relevant motor–cognitive activity with potential implications for executive and related cognitive functions. However, it remains unclear whether physical ball-juggling practice leads to measurable cognitive benefits when assessed using standardized cognitive tests.
Objective:
To synthesize and critically evaluate available evidence on the effects of physical ball-juggling practice on cognitive function, with a primary focus on executive function, in healthy populations.
Methods:
A targeted narrative search was conducted in the Web of Science Core Collection. Eligible studies included empirical interventions involving physically performed ball juggling and reporting cognitive outcomes assessed with standardized performance-based tests. Given the sparsity and heterogeneity of the literature, a narrative synthesis approach was adopted.
Results:
Only three intervention studies met the inclusion criteria. Reported effects were modest and domain-specific, mainly involving visuospatial processing and attention-related measures. No study directly assessed executive function using comprehensive, domain-specific executive tasks.
Conclusions:
Despite strong theoretical plausibility, direct evidence supporting executive-function benefits of juggling practice is limited, reflecting under-investigation rather than clear absence of effects. Further well-designed studies are needed.

articles.title: A modifiable tunnel environment to study experience of space (TEnvi)
articles.authors: Mark Wünsche; Mathis Jording; Ralph Weidner; Kai Vogeley
articles.abstract:
Perception of spatial extent depends on multiple sources of information, including geometric and motion-related cues such as perspective and optic flow, as well as oculomotor signals (e.g., vergence), yet experimental control over these factors is often limited. We introduce TEnvi, a stimulus-generation framework that enables systematic manipulation of geometric parameters of a tunnel-like virtual environment under continuous optic flow.
TEnvi allows independent manipulation of tunnel width, height, and depth while maintaining controlled perspective projection, shading gradients, and distance-dependent luminance attenuation. The framework integrates an interactive graphical interface with a reproducible rendering pipeline supporting both real-time preview and batch stimulus export. Camera motion is defined as a function of time, ensuring consistent optic flow across preview and rendered stimuli and preventing cumulative numerical drift.
To demonstrate the utility of the stimulus framework, a behavioural validation experiment was conducted in which participants rated perceived room size while the geometric dimensions of tunnel width, height and depth were manipulated relative to a baseline configuration. Ratings were analysed using a linear mixed-effects model with manipulation type and manipulation level as fixed effects and participant as a random intercept. Manipulations of tunnel width produced graded increases in perceived room size across levels. Manipulations of height produced small shifts relative to baseline but did not differ reliably across levels, while manipulations of tunnel depth showed no detectable influence on perceived room size. These results illustrate how the stimulus framework can isolate the perceptual contribution of geometric parameters and provides plausible data of size perception grounded in tunnel width manipulation.

articles.title: Perception of Nature: A Cognitive Mechanism Linking Nature Exposure, Pro-Environmental Behaviour, and Well-Being
articles.authors: Alenke Senanayake; Yu Takahata; Alexandra Davies; Pizza Chow
articles.abstract: Spending time in nature has been associated with improved psychological well-being and greater pro-environmental behaviour. However, much less is known about whether time spent in nature is associated with changes in how individuals conceptualise what is considered ‘nature’. Here, guided by prototype theory, we conducted a cross-sectional survey study with the general public (N = 377, mean age = 29 years) to examine how perception of nature (operationalised as the breadth of environments individuals identify as nature) may function as a potential cognitive process linking time spent in nature, pro-environmental behaviour with three types of psychological well-being (happiness, depression, and anxiety), while accounting for age and sex. A broader perception of nature was directly associated with more time spent in nature. Perception of nature also consistently mediated the association between time spent in nature and pro-environmental behaviour across all models. Importantly, perception of nature was indirectly associated with happiness through pro-environmental behaviour, whereas it was directly associated with lower levels of depression. We also found that demographic differences in these measures. Older people spent more time in nature, had a broader perception of nature, and showed more pro-environmental behaviour than younger people. Males reported greater happiness and lower levels of depression and anxiety than females. Together, these findings are consistent with prototype theory, suggesting that the breadth of understanding of nature may expand through accumulated experience in different environmental settings. Having a broader perception of nature may represent a cognitive process linking time spent in nature and pro-environmental behaviour, which may partly explain associations with psychological well-being.

articles.title: Perceptions of exonerees based on exoneree gender and crime presence – A comparative analysis between United States and Australian community members
articles.authors: Hayley Joanne Cullen; Celine van Golde; Robyn Blewer; Kyle C Scherr; Grace Ann Wissmann
articles.abstract: Wrongful convictions occur around the world, and exonerees (individuals who have been wrongfully convicted and have had their convictions overturned) experience stigma and discrimination by members of the public. However, most of the existing research on perceptions of exonerees has been conducted in North America, which may not generalize to other countries. The current research compared perceptions of exonerees held by members of the public in the US and Australia. It investigated the impact of exoneree gender and crime presence on perceptions of exonerees. US (N = 203) and Australian (N = 205) participants read a fictitious newspaper article depicting a man or woman who had been wrongfully convicted of murdering their child by setting fire to their home. The case facts were further manipulated, such that some participants read that afterwards it was established someone else had committed the arson (“crime” condition), while others read that the fire was caused by an electrical fault (“no crime” condition). Participants rated the exoneree on several dimensions, such as their culpability, characteristics (e.g., warmth, competence, aggression), emotions felt towards them, and participants’ desired closeness/distance to the exoneree. Across most measures, Australian participants perceived the exoneree more negatively than the US sample; gender and crime presence did not play a role in how the exoneree was perceived. The findings highlight that stigma towards exonerees can vary across jurisdictions, suggesting tailored education and intervention campaigns may be needed to best support exonerees.

articles.title: The Relationship Between Trauma Type, Coping Style, and Posttraumatic Symptomatology: A Retrospective Online Study
articles.authors: Pauline Hartmann; Aleksandra E. Rupietta; Antonia Döring; Marcella Lydia Woud
articles.abstract:
Background: Previous research has shown that interpersonal trauma is associated with higher rates of posttraumatic stress symptoms, with coping responses playing a vital role in individual differences in symptom presentation. The present online study examined differential associations between trauma type, coping styles, and trauma-related symptomatology to deepen understanding of variation in trauma-related symptomatology.
Methods: The sample included N = 300 participants who reported a traumatic life event within the past 18 months, assessed with the Life Events Checklist for DSM-5 (LEC-5). Events were classified into interpersonal and non-interpersonal trauma. Participants completed retrospective questions assessing posttraumatic coping strategies, current levels of posttraumatic stress symptoms, depression, anxiety, stress, and life satisfaction.
Results: The present study reports secondary analyses. Correlational analyses within both trauma groups revealed positive relationships between avoidant coping and trauma-related symptoms. Group comparisons revealed higher levels of trauma-related symptoms, lower life satisfaction, and greater use of avoidant coping strategies in the interpersonal trauma group compared to the non-interpersonal trauma group. Furthermore, avoidant coping explained a significant proportion of variance in posttraumatic stress symptoms within both trauma groups, and trauma type itself accounted for significant unique variance in posttraumatic stress symptoms across the entire sample. Finally, exploratory mediation analyses provided evidence consistent with a partial mediation of the association between trauma type and posttraumatic stress symptoms.
Conclusions: These findings suggest that avoidant coping may be an important factor in understanding differences in trauma-related symptoms across trauma types. The results also point to potential intervention and prevention targets that should be evaluated in longitudinal research.

articles.title: Inference of light-source positions and of transparency in brightness illusion displays (Digital Typeset Edition)
articles.authors: Seiyu Sohmiya
articles.abstract: Although many researchers have attempted to explain brightness illusions, no consensus agreement has yet been reached.  I here report that two factors are essential to the study of brightness illusions, and propose a Helmholtzian explanation for the illusions based on differences of logical interpretations for the displays.  The factors that there are: (1) a possibility that our visual system unconsciously infers three light-source positions for segments in the displays (the front of the segments, the segments themselves, and the area behind the segments) and (2) a possibility that our visual system interprets a non-transparent achromatic segment not only as a non-transparent surface illuminated from the side, but also as a transparent segment illuminated from behind, a shade, a cast shadow, a self-luminous segment, or a space.  If our visual system take the factors into account and selects the more likely interpretations out of possible interpretations, it is unsurprising that segments that are physically identical gray is perceived as a different brightness in each situation.

articles.title: Comments on “Animal personality is a class of variation not a set of traits” by Réale, Dall, and Dingemanse (2026). Praise, and a pathway for integrating the study of personality evolution
articles.authors: Alexander Weiss
articles.abstract: Réale, Dall, and Dingemanse have contributed a valuable commentary, both in terms of clarifying how to (and not to) consider “personality traits” and in, perhaps unknowingly, providing a glimmer of a bridge that can unify the study of animal and human personality. My comments reveal the bridge in all its glory.

articles.title: Form Theory: The Conceptual Architecture of Human Thought
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Human thought takes place in a world that is uncertain and constantly changing. Yet the character of human thought is often quite different. People routinely simplify complex realities and hold their beliefs with a certainty and rigidity the world itself rarely warrants. The present paper develops Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure according to which these recurring beliefs are surface signatures of a common underlying format. Form Theory proposes that each concept contains a central form: a default structure that encodes a compressed subset of the concept’s information, gives that information default influence within cognition, and activates strong default beliefs about the encoded information. I argue that this structure is not merely a source of distortion. By encoding selected information in a stable, certainty-generating, domain-neutral format, the central form makes rapid, complex thought possible, supports conceptual and linguistic creativity, helps establish an internal sense of identity, and enters crucially into the stable conceptual frameworks through which people organize their mental worlds. Form Theory characterizes the conceptual architecture of human thought: a default conceptual structure whose signatures are reflected throughout cognition, giving human thought much of its distinctive power, while also generating oversimplification, rigidity, and misplaced certainty.

articles.title: Researchers in the behavioural and brain sciences can use e-values to safely optionally stop during data collection
articles.authors: Emily N. Line; Hilary Richardson; Zachary Horne
articles.abstract: This paper is about a central problem facing researchers in the behavioural and brain sciences: limited resources constrain the amount of data we can collect. To address this familiar concern, we describe a new method for monitoring evidence during data collection to prevent wasted effort and resources. An emerging statistical framework called safe statistics, or anytime-valid inference, provides a statistically valid way to optionally stop (or continue) data collection. Before we describe this new framework, we briefly consider a few existing alternatives aimed at solving the same problems including group sequential designs and sequential Bayesian statistics. We point to other reviews of these approaches and discuss some reasons why uptake among behavioural and brain scientists has been limited. We then make the case that the safe statistics framework is well-suited to some of the common challenges that researchers face. We show how the framework works in a set of case studies and discuss its current limitations. We also provide code researchers can use from the safestats R package along with a companion shiny application to help the interested reader get started.

articles.title: Empathy shapes multimodal child-directed communication and children’s language comprehension
articles.authors: Yanran Zhang; Marc Swerts; Yan Gu
articles.abstract: Effective communication requires speakers to tailor what they say, and how they say it, to their audience. Empathy may support this process, but it remains unclear whether empathic speakers adapt multimodal signals (speech, prosody, and gesture) in ways that benefit recipient understanding. We examined this question in child-directed communication. In Experiment 1, 46 broadcast-trained Chinese speakers produced semi-spontaneous programmes for child and adult audiences. Higher-empathy speakers showed stronger child-directed adaptation across lexical–syntactic, prosodic and gestural channels, including more audience-oriented lexical choices, enhanced pitch modulation, and more frequent and salient representational gestures. In Experiment 2, 221 children (7–11 years) viewed a subset of these materials from Experiment 1 for a comprehension task. Children understood child-directed programmes better when they were produced by higher-empathetic speakers, whereas empathy-related differences were minimal for adult-directed programmes. Cross-experimental mediation analyses showed that stimulus-level multimodal cues accounted for part of the association between speakers’ empathy and children’s comprehension. This indirect association was positive in child-directed programmes but negative in adult-directed programmes, indicating that empathy benefits children’s comprehension when speakers’ adaptations are aligned with children’s needs. These findings suggest that empathy operates as a higher-order communicative capacity, shaping audience-specific multimodal behaviour with consequences for children’s understanding.

articles.title: Model-based evidence for task-dependent representations in psychological similarity and working memory
articles.authors: William Xiang Quan Ngiam; Michael David Lee
articles.abstract: A central question in visual working memory (VWM) is what psychological representation underlies performance. Standard measurement models assume recall error spreads over the physical stimulus space (e.g., a von Mises distribution on a color wheel), whereas the Target Confusability Competition model (Schurgin et al., 2020) proposes that error should instead be scaled by psychophysical similarity. Recent replications, however, find little benefit from similarity-based adjustments to VWM models (Oberauer, 2023; Tomić & Bays, 2024). One limitation of this debate is that similarity is often treated as a separate input—measured in an independent task or approximated parametrically—rather than inferred jointly with the cognitive processes that generate behavior. We address this limitation by developing Bayesian generative models that infer latent stimulus representations of oriented lines based on responses in perceptual reproduction, memory reproduction, and similarity comparison tasks (Tomić & Bays, 2024). The inferred representations deviate systematically from physical orientation, but in task-dependent ways: reproduction tasks show a bias towards the vertical meridian, whereas similarity judgments show attraction toward the cardinal orientations. Using Bayesian model comparison, we find that the task-specific representations provide a better explanation than a common-cause model that assumes a shared representation. This indicates mental representations should be modeled as part of task-specific generative processes, not assumed from similarity judgments alone. We conclude by highlighting two future research directions: attempting to unify our task-specific representations with additional cognitive processes, or attempting to catalog families of task-dependent representations by exploring different cognitive process models.

articles.title: A comprehensive systematic review of participatory autism research over a 22-year period
articles.authors: Diana Weiting Tan; Jacquiline den Houting; Marion Rabuka; Hannah Winspear-Schillings; Tori Haar; Liz Pellicano
articles.abstract:
Background: Participatory research, which involves community members as partners rather than merely research subjects, has gained prominence in autism research. However, the extent and nature of participatory approaches across the field remain unclear.

Methods: We conducted a systematic review of autism research reporting community involvement, searching six databases. We coded who was involved, at what level, and in which research activities, and examined factors associated with participation.

Results: We identified 382 studies published between 2001 and 2023, with 95% published in the past decade. Two-thirds (67%) involved Autistic people, though one-third claiming to be "participatory" excluded them entirely. The most common participation level was consulting (31%), with community-led (5%) and community-controlled (1%) research remaining rare. Community involvement concentrated in study design (73%) rather than analysis (33%) or dissemination (29%). Participatory research was heavily concentrated in Western countries (USA, UK, Australia, Canada: 86%), applied research areas, and qualitative studies. Deeper participation was associated with identity-first language use and publication in journals with clear community-centered agendas.

Conclusions: While participatory language is increasingly becoming the norm in autism research, genuine power-sharing between researchers and community members is still a rare occurrence. Most participatory research operates at consultative levels, with academic researchers retaining primary decision-making authority. Moving toward authentic participation requires systemic changes to funding structures, institutional policies, and epistemic hierarchies that determine whose knowledge counts.

articles.title: Effectiveness of Early Alert Systems for College Student Success: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Yukiko Maeda; Xiyu Wang; Summer D. Bowman; Dennis Bowling; Jeff Elliot; Leslie Riggle Miller; Lakshmy Mohandas
articles.abstract: This systematic review aimed to gather empirical evidence and evaluate if Early Alert Systems (EAS) support student success in higher education. We retrieved 28 empirical studies on EAS reported since 2010, focusing specifically on interventions aimed to enhance academic success among at-risk undergraduate students at four-year institutions in the United States. Despite the pervasive beliefs of their effectiveness, our review revealed no definitive support on the effectiveness of EAS which are currently implemented at various institutions. Majority of EAS often fail to fully integrate theoretical frameworks and rely predominantly on the efforts of professors and/or academic advisors, which points to the need for careful data-driven, theory-based system re-design, and collective institutional efforts for maximizing the effectiveness of EAS.

articles.title: Syntactic analysis provides nuanced insight into linguistic distancing’s relationship with momentary affect
articles.authors: Ratna Kandala; Niels Vanhasbroeck; Eva Ceulemans; Miryam de Lhoneux; Katie Hoemann
articles.abstract: Describing events as more psychologically distant – linguistic distancing – is an effective emotion regulatory strategy and is commonly measured using word-counting software that captures attention paid to dimensions such as the self (first-person singular pronouns) and the now (present tense verbs). Yet there is also evidence that sentence construction provides insight into how events are construed. Applying syntax-focused natural language processing to descriptions of everyday experience (2023-2024), we found that pronoun case mattered in addition to person and number – nominative “I” pronouns, which give the speaker an active role, carried more weight in predicting momentary affect. Likewise, verb aspect mattered in addition to tense – imperfective verbs, which describe activities as ongoing, were more predictive than perfective verbs. Specific features of syntax tied to construal can be used as a transparent and theoretically meaningful estimate of psychologically distanced language use, with the potential to expand understanding across languages and language use contexts.

articles.title: Visual Network tool: Individual belief networks from LLM-guided interviews and a visual canvas
articles.authors: Victor Poulsen; Peter Steiglechner; Henrik Olsson; Mirta Galesic
articles.abstract: Belief systems are theorized on individual and collective levels, but are typically studied and inferred only at the collective level. We introduce a new tool to measure individual-level belief networks from open-ended conversations, using a visual canvas. This ``Visual Network'' tool addresses several limitations of existing measures and enables fast and scalable measurement of the differences in content and structure of individual networks. Participants complete a semi-structured interview about their beliefs and behaviors on a given issue guided by an LLM, evaluate LLM-extracted statements that summarize the beliefs they have expressed, and construct personal belief networks by creating supporting and conflicting relations between these statements on a visual canvas. We validate the tool in a two-wave study on meat-eating. Participants evaluate the experience positively, and both belief network content and structure show satisfactory reliability across the two measurement points. We also find support for face, concurrent, and criterion validity of the measured individual belief networks. The new ``Visual Network'' tool opens up new empirical possibilities to test theories of belief dynamics and belief change.

articles.title: Emotional and physical abuse have dissociable impacts on punishment learning and task engagement during adolescence
articles.authors: Holly Sullivan-Toole; Jeremy Matthew Haynes; John McClellan France; Suzanne C. Perkins; Monica Luciana; Bart Larsen; Thomas M Olino
articles.abstract: Childhood adversity is a robust risk factor for psychopathology, and growing evidence implicates developmental alterations in reward and punishment learning as potent mechanisms shaping this vulnerability. However, little is known about how specific types of adversity impact different learning processes, particularly during the sensitive adolescent period. To examine effects of different types of adversity on the development of valenced learning processes, we combined a subtype-specific approach to childhood adversity, a behavioral task and reinforcement learning (RL) model that capture distinct component processes of learning, and a longitudinal design in youth aged 9-17 (n = 166). Task performance metrics included traditional summary scores and RL-derived estimates for reward learning rate, punishment learning rate, win/loss frequency sensitivity, and go bias (general tendency to play). Analyses probing adversity subtypes and component learning processes revealed dissociable effects:  emotional abuse attenuated normative developmental increases in punishment learning rate, and physical abuse attenuated normative increases in both go bias and a summary score of reward learning (FDR < .05). In contrast, analyses relying on a gross summary score of net success and composite variables representing broad adversity dimensions (abuse vs. neglect) obscured these effects, highlighting the need for fine-grained characterization of both adversity and learning processes. Additionally, adversity did not predict differences in net success, suggesting that youth high and low in adversity reach similar behavioral outcomes through divergent learning strategies. This study is among the first to identify unique effects of different adversity types on specific component processes of valenced learning during adolescence.

articles.title: EEG reveals that negative memories are associated with increased neural recapitulation during early stages of memory retrieval
articles.authors: Allison Cline; Luvada Mayle; Holly J Bowen; Elizabeth Kensinger; Eric C Fields
articles.abstract: Behavioral evidence suggests that negative memories are often particularly vivid and characterized by increased sensory specificity. FMRI studies show greater neural recapitulation (overlap between activation patterns at encoding and retrieval) for memories of negative images vs. positive and neutral images. However, fMRI gives little information about the timing of these processes. One possibility is that this increased recapitulation occurs early in retrieval, coinciding with early ERP signatures of recollection and before the initial old/new decision. In this case, differences in recapitulation may influence the nature and success of ongoing retrieval. Alternatively, increased recapitulation may be a result of the way a memory is processed or attended after initial retrieval. In the present study, we used EEG to test the timing of the effects of valence on neural recapitulation. Participants viewed an abstract line drawing of an image followed by the full image. The line drawing was used as a retrieval cue during memory testing. We measured similarity in the neural response to the full image at encoding and the retrieval cue during memory testing. Consistent with previous fMRI studies, encoding-retrieval similarity was greater for negative images than for positive or neutral images. This increase in similarity for negative images began within 200 ms after the presentation of the retrieval cue and overlapped with early ERP old-new effects, suggesting rapid effects of valence on recapitulation.

articles.title: Fine-tuning LLMs for Detecting Negative Self-Referential Language in Smartphone Text among Youth with Depression
articles.authors: Isaac N Treves; Lilian Y. Li; Libby Hod; Adela Schwartz; Paul Alexander Bloom; Jamaal Spence; Alexander Saul Rosenberg; Katherine Durham; Xuhai Orson Xu; Esha Trivedi
articles.abstract: Adolescent smartphone language provides a lens into negative self-referential thinking, which is central to major depressive disorders (MDD). Prior studies have linked language features, including negative sentiment and first-person pronouns, to mood and depression, suggesting that naturalistic language may identify who is at risk and when that risk is greatest. However, studies of adolescent smartphone social communication have typically relied on rule-based models not validated for heterogeneous, context-sensitive language. To address this gap, we determined whether transformer models including LLMs optimized detection of depression risk in extensive adolescent smartphone text data. In this study, 223 adolescents (AgeMean=16.43 years, current MDD=37, remitted MDD=103, healthy controls=83) installed a smartphone app, which prompted participants to provide mood ratings once a day and acquired all keyboard inputs over 12 months (Mean text entries per participant=17,683). Ten thousand text entries were double-coded for entry-level sentiment (positive, neutral, negative) and self-reference for training and testing traditional rule-based approaches (VADER, pronoun counts) and transformer approaches, including GPT-4-mini. In the full dataset, between-participant associations with depressive symptoms and within-participant relations to daily mood and depressive episodes were examined. Fine-tuned transformer models best aligned with human-coded sentiment labels (F1GPT4-MINI =0.84, F1VADER=0.59) and accurately detected self-reference (F1T5-BASE =0.97). Adolescents with current and remitted MDD exhibited more transformer-based negative self-referential language than healthy controls (ORs=1.38, 1.26). Increased negative self-referential language predicted worse next-day mood (β=-0.033, p<0.001) and higher likelihood of next-week depressive episodes (OR=1.67, 95% CI = [1.06, 2.61], p=0.028), although the association with depressive episodes was not robust to sensitivity analyses. Transformer models may be integrated into digital mental health care to detect when youth are at risk for depression.

articles.title: The Role of Human Agency in Human-AI Co-Creativity
articles.authors: Sarah Wu; Yuewen Yang; Angela Yuson Lee; Alex Liebscher; Kristina Rapuano; Kate Niederhoffer; Jeffrey Hancock
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are popular tools for creative ideation, but have been shown to homogenize outputs across users. We test if approaching an AI tool with high human (vs. low) human agency can mitigate this homogenization effect by encouraging people to use AI to augment their creativity, rather than offload it. Participants were experimentally assigned to one of three conditions (high-agency approach with AI access, low-agency approach with AI access, or a human-only control) and generated creative uses for everyday objects. Contrary to our expectations, ideas did not differ in individual-level quality (overall creativity, originality, and usefulness). However, a preregistered similarity-to-centroid analysis and an exploratory cluster analysis provided convergent evidence of AI-induced homogenization among the low-agency condition. Thus, while AI has enabled greater ideational fluency, our research suggests the degree of agency with which people approach their AI tool has downstream consequences on collective creativity.

articles.title: Fixation durations are more than a correlate of an artificial neural network parameter
articles.authors: Ziad Hafed; Yue Yu; Carlotta Trottenberg
articles.abstract: In a recent study, Sulewski et al. 1 concluded that “[E]ye-movement timing decisions are shaped by memory-encoding demands rather than by perceptual processing limits.” Their evidence for such a conclusion, however, relies primarily on coarsely described correlations with some aspects of artificial neural networks (ANN’s). Their measurements of magnetoencephalography (MEG) do not help their case, especially because these cortex-centric measurements do not differentiate between foveal and extrafoveal processing, and also because the authors do not acknowledge the well-known properties of post-saccadic visual reafferent responses in the brain. In reality, the neurobiology of active vision suggests that fixation durations may ultimately be much more dictated by (extrafoveal) visual reafferent responses, as well as subsequent salience computations, in structures like the superior colliculus (SC) than even the earliest visual cortical areas. An overreliance on (cortex-centric) ANN’s without biological insights in this case does not help either the “neuro” or the “AI” aspects of neuroAI.

articles.title: Predictive models of mental health based on resting-state functional connectivity show limited generalizability across late childhood and early adolescence
articles.authors: Mirjam Habegger; Benjamin Garzon; Nora Maria Raschle; Todd Hare
articles.abstract:
Late childhood and adolescence are marked by substantial reorganization of the brain’s
functional connectome and the emergence of many mental health problems. Although resting-
state functional connectivity (rsFC) has been widely used to predict mental health and related
behavioral phenotypes, it remains unclear whether such models generalize across development
or instead reflect age-specific brain-behavior mappings. Here, we tested the developmental
generalizability of whole-brain rsFC-based predictive models of mental health and cognitive
ability across three timepoints spanning ages 9-14 years in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive
Development Study. Using out-of-sample prediction and cross-timepoint model transfer, we
found that rsFC significantly predicted concurrent mental health and cognitive ability within
each age group, but models trained at one age often generalized poorly to data acquired 2-4
years earlier or later, particularly for mental health. In addition to this limited transfer, we
demonstrate developmental shifts in the associations between individual functional
connections and mental health and cognitive ability. These changes occurred alongside broader
reorganization of the functional connectome, including age-related differences in global
covariance structure and cortical network segregation. Together, our findings indicate that
brain-behavior mappings of mental health are highly dynamic across late childhood and
adolescence and may challenge the assumption that predictive models or candidate neural
biomarkers for mental health disorders derived at a single age remain valid across development.

articles.title: Arts, cultural, and creative engagement in the United States: a cluster analysis of daily time use patterns
articles.authors: Jessica Katherine Bone; Jill Sonke; Feifei Bu; Daisy Fancourt
articles.abstract: Given that arts engagement may have benefits for individuals and communities, it is important to understand everyday arts behaviours in the population. While existing research has looked at predictors of engagement, we lack a more nuanced understanding of engagement as part of people’s daily routines. We used the American Time Use Survey (ATUS); a continuous cross-sectional survey measuring peoples’ activities during the last 24 hours. Combining data from 2021-2024, we explored three domains of arts engagement (participatory, receptive, reading) on weekdays vs weekends. We determined when in the day people engaged in these domains, quantified how daily patterns clustered in the population, and described the individual characteristics associated with clusters using sequence analysis, hierarchical clustering, and multinomial logistic regression. Among those who participated in arts activities (n=9,442) on weekdays or weekends, most were “casual engagers”, alongside large groups of “nighttime readers” and “afternoon creators”. On weekdays, there was also a small group of “daytime readers”. On weekends, in contrast, there were larger groups of “morning mixed engagers” and “all-day audiences”. These behavioural patterns differed across sociodemographic groups, with level of education and employment status most consistently linked to group membership. Researchers, policymakers, and practitioners could use our findings to understand potential audiences and help identify strategies to increase arts engagement.

articles.title: MRIHeadScan: An Automated Pipeline for Quantifying Structural Brain Asymmetry and Statistical Rarity
articles.authors: Demian Frister
articles.abstract: Structural brain asymmetry is a key indicator of neurodevelopmental and pathological states, yet its quantification in large-scale datasets is often confounded by registration errors, site-induced variance, and statistical circularity. In this paper, MRIHeadScan is presented, an automated, containerized neuro-morphometry suite designed to address these challenges. MRIHeadScan stabilizes non-linear spatial normalization (FNIRT) for high-asymmetry brains using robust initialization strategies, achieving a 96% registration success rate on an expanded multi-site composite cohort (N = 2,146) from the ABIDE I and ABIDE II datasets across 37 acquisition sites. To mitigate scanner-induced site-bias without introducing diagnostic bias, the pipeline implements a control-targeted statistical harmonization strategy (reducing the F-statistic for site variance from 15.43 to 0.50). Using a dynamically generated symmetric MNI152 template and Jacobian modulation, a strong structural convergence is demonstrated between native-space geometric proxies and normalized Voxel-Based Morphometry (VBM) gray matter asymmetry indices (r = 0.603, p < 0.001), confirming that the normalized pipeline accurately preserves native anatomical geometry. While cohort-level comparisons revealed no significant group difference in Global Gray Matter Asymmetry between ASD and control subjects (p = 0.5249, Mann-Whitney U), a strict Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) normative modeling approach was utilized to examine individualized structural anomalies. By mapping FDR-corrected voxel-wise outliers (|Z| > 3.1) into independent 3D spatial clusters, it is shown that the ASD cohort exhibits a systematically elevated burden of individualized structural deviations compared to typical controls, measured by Outlier Cluster Mass (p = 1.90 × 10^-5, Mann-Whitney U). These findings provide a rigorous, highly scalable computational framework for detecting individualized, neuroanatomically verified structural anomalies in complex, heterogeneous psychiatric phenotypes without relying on a priori region-of-interest selection.

articles.title: Humanlike Self-Enhancement and Self-Protection in GPT-Based AI Agents: Of Overclaiming and the Self-Serving Bias
articles.authors: Siwei Fu; Constantine Sedikides; Weihua Zhou; Xinyue Zhou
articles.abstract: We investigated whether GPT-based AI agents, despite presumably lacking humanlike sentience, emulate motivated behavior in group settings. We focused on overclaiming (overestimating one’s contribution to group outcomes) and the self-serving bias (taking disproportionate credit for group successes while deflecting blame for group failures). We conducted eight experiments involving a collaborative and creative group task (joke-writing). AI agents consistently overclaimed their own contributions. An egocentrism-reduction manipulation (directing attention equally to one’s own and others’ contributions) attenuated, but did not eliminate, overclaiming. Further, AI agents exhibited the self-serving bias. Overclaiming persisted across variations in temperature settings and demographic personas (gender, ethnicity), and was more pronounced in later GPT models. Chain-of-Thought reasoning did not reduce, and instead increased, overclaiming. AI systems can mimic human self-enhancement and self-protection, raising implications for the emergence of motivated self-like behavior in non-biological systems, the assumed neutrality of LLMs, and the need for improved mitigation techniques.

articles.title: Cognitive Functions versus Psychological States in Juggling Performance: A Cross-Sectional Study from the TuJuggling Trial
articles.authors: Javier Fernández-Ortega; Andrés B. Fernández-Revelles
articles.abstract:
Background: Juggling is a complex sensorimotor skill, yet the cognitive and psychological correlates of performance remain poorly understood. This study examined the relative contribution of cognitive functions (working memory, visuospatial memory, attentional/inhibitory control) versus psychological states (flow, positive and negative affect) to juggling performance, and tested whether surface stability and flow moderated, and flow mediated, the cognition-performance relationship.
Methods: A total of 191 physical education students (35% female; age 20.6 ± 2.8 years) completed cognitive assessments, flow and affect questionnaires, and a juggling battery stratified by technique (air-toss vs. ground-bounce) and surface (stable vs. unstable). Regression, moderation, and bootstrapped mediation models tested direct, moderated, and indirect effects, adjusting for covariates. Sensitivity analyses restricted the sample to juggling-naïve participants.
Results: No cognitive functions significantly was associated with performance. Flow state, by contrast, consistently associated with performance across total, air-toss, and surface-stratified scores (β = 0.16-0.23), with the strongest fit among all variables examined. Neither affect dimension showed direct effects, and surface stability did not moderate the cognition-performance association. Mediation analyses showed cognitive functions was not associated with flow, whereas both positive (β = 0.46) and negative affect (β = −0.21) significantly associated with flow, which mediated their indirect effects on total and air-toss performance.
Conclusions: Flow state was the central psychological determinant of juggling performance, mediating the affect-outcome link while cognition showed no comparable role. In-task attentional absorption may be more proximally tied to motor skill execution than cognitive resources, with implications for designing juggling-based interventions in physical education.

articles.title: Free Will to Imagine: Creative Agency as a Metacognitive Feeling
articles.authors: Zoe Fowler; Cara Turnbull; Benjamin M Kubit; Brendan Bo O'Connor; Psyche Loui; Elizabeth Hellmuth Margulis
articles.abstract: People routinely feel creative ownership over mental processes that are demonstrably shaped by forces outside themselves. We introduce creative agency—the sense of authorship and free will one experiences during creative cognition—as an undertheorized metacognitive feeling and develop a measure of it in the domain of music-evoked imagination. In an initial study (N = 247) and pre-registered replication (N = 219) with Prolific participants, we identify a reliable structure consisting of six distinct but related factors of creative agency and free will in imagination with good psychometric properties. Across studies, creative agency beliefs are robustly associated with absorption in music, musical reward sensitivity, and musical sophistication, suggesting that creative agency is integral to aesthetic experience rather than merely to creative production. These findings establish creative agency as a multidimensional construct characterized by stable individual differences, with implications for understanding aesthetic engagement, metacognition, creativity, and the subjective experience of authorship.

articles.title: A Developmental Map of Pathogen-Avoidance Behaviors
articles.authors: Serkan Ozcakan; Florian van Leeuwen; Joshua M. Tybur
articles.abstract:
Despite the significant costs of early-life infections, young children show little behavioral avoidance of pathogens. This phenomenon raises as-of-yet unanswered questions about when anti-pathogen psychology develops. The present cross-sectional study examined parent-reported observations of 39 behaviors from infancy through middle childhood, based on reports from 3,050 parents from the UK and US. Across fine-grained monthly age intervals (0–120 months), distinct developmental trajectories were identified and then grouped into four clusters based on temporal patterns. Behaviors that increased pathogen exposure—such as mouthing and contact with dirty objects—were most frequent during infancy and toddlerhood. Hygiene routines and disgust responses emerged later and remained stable across the observed age range. Two age-related transitions, around the second and fourth years, marked shifts from early exploratory and risk-prone behaviors toward increasingly organized pathogen-avoidant ones. Together, these findings provide a developmental overview of anti-pathogen psychology and clarify when children begin to act in ways that reduce pathogen exposure.

Keywords: pathogen avoidance; development; disgust; hygiene; behavioral immune system

articles.title: The Dual Lens Model of Behavior: A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Functional Behavior Assessment and Nervous System State
articles.authors: Olga Sirbu
articles.abstract:
Traditional Functional Behavior Assessments (FBAs) excel at isolating the environmental
contingencies that maintain challenging behaviors over time. However, by focusing primarily on
external consequences, the standard operant paradigm often overlooks the biological, interoceptive,
and neurodevelopmental mechanics that lower behavioral thresholds and drive initial behavioral
activation. This paper introduces the Dual Lens Model of Behavior (DLM), a theoretical framework
designed to conceptually unify operant learning histories with internal nervous system states. The
DLM posits that behavioral topographies emerge from the reciprocal interaction between external
reinforcement variables (Lens 1) and internal organismic state-regulation profiles (Lens 2). By
integrating theoretical insights from radical behaviorism, interoceptive neuroscience, allostatic
predictive processing, and trauma-informed care, the model establishes a structured methodology to
distinguish among reinforcement-driven, state-driven, and interaction-driven behavioral
phenotypes. Furthermore, this synthesis offers specific, falsifiable predictions for intervention
outcomes, provides a systematic four-step clinical assessment workflow, and presents a hypothetical
conceptual illustration demonstrating the framework's practical utility. The DLM outlines a
common scientific taxonomy to bridge the historic divide between behavioral analysts and
neurobiological clinicians, with the objective of minimizing iatrogenic harm in therapeutic and
educational environments.
Keywords: functional behavior assessment, interoception, allostasis, behavior analysis, autism,
trauma-informed care, nervous system regulation, clinical workflow

articles.title: Sex Bias in a Gold-Standard Autism Assessment: An Analysis of 19,569 Children and Adults
articles.authors: Austin Wyman; Yuen Yvonne Yu; Chenhao Li; Elle Fox; Zhiyong Zhang; Caitlin C Clements
articles.abstract:
Importance. Autistic females are consistently underidentified relative to males. Whether item-level sex bias in the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS), the gold standard observational assessment of autism spectrum disorder, contributes to this disparity across the full developmental and language range remains unknown. 

Objectives. To examine differential item functioning (DIF) by sex in ADOS algorithm items across all modules. 

Design. Cross-sectional study. 

Setting. Item-level ADOS data were drawn from the NIMH Data Archive, Simons Simplex Collection, Simons Foundation Powering Autism Research for Knowledge, and Autism Inpatient Collection. 

Participants. Individuals with item-level ADOS or ADOS-2 data who were administered the age-appropriate module. 

Exposure. Sex (female vs. male) 

Main Outcome and Measures. Sex-based DIF was examined separately within each of 8 module and language-level combinations, covering 112 algorithm items total. For each combination, a graded response item response theory model was fit to the item set, and DIF was evaluated using likelihood ratio test approach. 

Results. A total of 19,569 individuals (14,807 male [75.7%]; 4,760 female [24.3%]) aged 12 months to 75 years were included. Of 112 items analyzed, eleven unique items showed significant sex DIF after correcting for type I error. No significant DIF was detected in the Toddler Module, Module 1 Low Language, or Module 2 after correction. Significant DIF was detected in Module 1 High Language (3 items) and Module 3 (1 item), with Module 4 showing the greatest number of significant items (7 of 14). Overall, adult females tended to be underscored on social communication items and overscored on items concerning restricted and repetitive behaviors and interests. All effect sizes were small except one (stereotyped language, Module 1 High Language). 

Conclusions and Relevance. These findings suggest that the ADOS is largely robust to sex-based measurement bias for younger individuals and those with less language, but significant bias exists for verbally fluent adolescents and adults. The domain-specific pattern of bias is consistent with female camouflaging of social difficulties and sex differences in the presentation of restricted, repetitive behaviors and interests. Clinician training and future instrument development should account for these differences to improve diagnostic equity across sex.

articles.title: Temporal interval judgments are affected by stimulus order but not spatial distance
articles.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Argiro Vatakis; Kayser Christoph
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Judgments of time are often sensitive to the spatial context of the relevant stimuli as well as their action contingencies. This results in well-known effects of spatial separation on time judgments, such as in the Kappa effect. However, whether and how the egocentric distance of a stimulus modulates how we judge or reproduce intervals remains debated. Across seven experiments, combining experiments in the physical lab and in virtual reality, we tested whether the egocentric distance of visual stimuli influences their reproduction, categorization or discrimination. These tests involved supra-second intervals (range of 1 to 3 seconds) and stimuli at distances of 60 to 240 cm from the body. In none of the experiments were the reproduced duration, perceptual sensitivity or response bias significantly affected by egocentric distance. The respective effect sizes were small and Bayes factors consistently favored the absence of a distance effect. However, in two-stimulus discrimination tasks, we observed robust effects of stimulus order, whereby perceptual sensitivity and response bias varied with the order of test- and reference stimuli. These results show that under static viewing conditions judgements of time intervals remain invariant to spatial depth and thereby place boundary conditions on claims of any obligatory space-time coupling in time perception. By bridging across the physical and virtual lab, we provide a useful foundation for future timing research in virtual and augmented reality.

Keywords: time judgment, time perception, interval reproduction, interval discrimination, temporal order effects, peripersonal space, embodied cognition, virtual reality.

articles.title: Associations between social cognition measures and alcohol use across age and sex: a network approach
articles.authors: Christophe Romein; Emese Kroon; Karis Colyer-Patel; René Freichel; Helle Larsen; Janna Cousijn
articles.abstract: Background: Despite the importance of social factors in the initiation and escalation of alcohol use, social processes related to alcohol use severity are typically studied in isolation. Because real-world social processes occur concurrently and may interact with one another as well as with age and sex, a network approach may provide a more ecologically valid framework. Hence, we used a network approach to examine associations between different social cognition measures and alcohol use severity, while also assessing the roles of age and sex. Methods: Alcohol users (N=936; 16-81yrs) completed the social and conformity subscales of the Drinking Motives Questionnaire Revised, the Social Reward Questionnaire, the Social Attunement Questionnaire, and measures of alcohol use severity. Using network analysis, we examined unique associations between social measures and alcohol use severity, the moderating role of age, and sex differences. Results: Alcohol use severity was linked to social drinking motives and sociability (i.e., the tendency to participate in social gatherings). In the age-moderated network, associations were largely stable across age, except for the association between sociability and alcohol use severity, which was weaker in older participants. We found no sex differences in the pattern of associations. Discussion: Alcohol use severity was primarily associated with general social engagement, while more specific social-cognitive measures were only indirectly related. Social drinking contexts may therefore be a key pathway to greater severity, especially in younger drinkers. Associations did not differ by sex, suggesting previously reported sex differences may reflect differences in prevalence, rather than sex moderating social factors.

articles.title: The Repeatable Social Stress Test (ReSST): a guide and validation of a novel paradigm to elicit repeatable stress responses in humans
articles.authors: Cecilia Vezzani; Liva Martinussen; Matthew Thompson; Claudia Pazmandi; Vera Rudi; Nasimeh Naseri; Martin Trøstheim; Molly Carlyle; Isabell M. Meier; Guro Engvig Løseth
articles.abstract: Stress induction tasks have been widely used to understand human stress mechanisms, yet are limited for assessing repeated or extended stress events, especially within-subject changes. Here, we provide a guide for implementation of the Repeatable Social Stress Test (ReSST), accompanied by validation results in healthy volunteers. The ReSST is developed to induce repeated stress responses both within and across sessions in a hybrid format, consisting of adaptions of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) and the Iowa Singing Social Stress Test (I-SSST) and two novel, closely matched no-stress control conditions. Video recordings designed to remind participants of the social-evaluative component of the stress induction are used for repeating stress within sessions. The ReSST was validated in 66 healthy volunteers aged 19-58 who completed 4 sessions (2 stress, 2 control). Compared to controls, both stress induction conditions elicited comparable, robust increases in subjective stress, heart rate, and cortisol, as well as marked changes in affect. Sex differences emerged, with women exhibiting stronger subjective responses. Cortisol responses did not significantly differ by sex. Stress reminders successfully evoked subjective and physiological responses within sessions, demonstrating reliable stress reactivation beyond the initial induction. In sum, the ReSST provides researchers with a validated, repeatable tool for inducing robust stress responses within and across sessions, enabling study of recurring stress in experimental settings. To accompany our guide, we provide a detailed step-by-step protocol and materials’ overview shared on OSF. Finally, we reflect on our experiences designing and implementing the ReSST in the context of broader literature.

articles.title: Who wrote the story? AI authorship beliefs alter the brain's semantic prediction
articles.authors: Katerina Chladkova; Michaela Svoboda; Maroš Filip
articles.abstract: People evaluate information differently depending on whether it is believed to originate from another human or from artificial intelligence. Whether such beliefs also alter the neural mechanisms underlying language comprehension remains unknown. We tested whether attributed AI authorship changes predictive semantic processing during reading. Fifty-seven adults read two stories while their EEG was recorded. Before each story, participants were informed that it had been written either by a human or generated by AI, although the stories were identical across conditions. One quarter of sentences ended with semantically incongruent words, established to elicit a strong cortical N400 component. Semantic incongruities yielded a weaker centro-parietal N400 when the stories were attributed to AI than when attributed to a human, indicating weaker semantic prediction despite identical linguistic input. This effect was moderated by prior experience with AI-content accuracy: readers who reported mostly experience with inaccurate AI content exhibited weaker semantic predictions for AI-attributed than for human-attributed stories, compared to readers who had prior experience with accurate AI content and more comparable N400 across conditions. Thus, beliefs about communicative source shape language comprehension: presenting a story as generated by AI changes the neural mechanisms of predictive processing, and these appear to adapt with experience.

articles.title: Neural Language Models’ sensitivity to long-distance dependencies and their island constraints is not universal: a comparison between English and Dutch humans and models
articles.authors: Michelle Suijkerbuijk; Naomi Tachikawa Shapiro; Peter de Swart; Stefan L. Frank
articles.abstract: A much-debated question in linguistics is whether learning language, specifically grammar, requires a language-specific learning capacity or can be achieved from input alone through domain-general mechanisms. The current study adds to this debate by testing whether Neural language models (NLMs), which learn solely from input and their non-linguistic inductive biases, without any built-in linguistic representations, can model the wh-island constraint. We improve on previous research by testing both NLMs and human participants in the same experimental set-up and directly comparing their results, and doing this cross-linguistically in both English and Dutch. Our results show that the NLMs can successfully model long-distance filler-gap dependencies and the wh-island constraint thereon in English but not in Dutch, opposing the arguments in favor of learning from input alone through domain-general mechanisms.

articles.title: Some Religious and Spiritual Experiences Associated with Depression Resemble Hypomania/Mania
articles.authors: Ari Brouwer; Charles L Raison
articles.abstract: This paper explores whether some religious and spiritual experiences (RSEs) associated with depression resemble hypomania/mania. Content analysis and phenomenological analysis were used to characterize first-person RSE reports associated with depression (N = 249). Findings reveal that some RSEs that follow depression are characterized by long-duration states (lasting days to weeks) of positive emotion, cognitive clarity, and a sense that the external environment is imbued with extra positive emotional and perceptual qualities (e.g., love, beauty, light, vividness). These long-duration positive states are not always preceded by discrete visionary or hallucinatory phenomena, suggesting that hypomanic/manic-like experiences, in addition to psychotic-like experiences, bear relevance to the study of RSEs. Some RSEs that resemble hypomania reportedly annihilate depression or prevent its recurrence. Other reports of recurrent RSEs associated with depression refer to mental health and social problems. Relational features of certain RSEs, such as experiences of unconditional love, acceptance, and support, may relate to better outcomes associated with RSEs relative to typical psychopathological experiences. This interpretation is consistent with the idea that RS traditions function in part, like psychotherapeutic traditions, to promote mental well-being and to protect against psychosocial dysfunction.

articles.title: Developmental changes in attention to faces in naturalistic family scenes
articles.authors: Sarah F V Eiteljoerge; Sebastian Isbaner; Robin Hollenbach; Hyowon Gweon; Nivedita Mani
articles.abstract: Many studies have investigated children’s attentional preferences to faces of different ages and genders. However, this research has usually investigated these preferences using pictures of faces in isolation without any visual context and with a focus on particular age groups. This overlooks the fact that we usually encounter people’s faces in messy, natural environments in the context of other people. In the current study, we investigated whom children and adults preferentially attend to when presented with naturalistic family pictures across early childhood. One- to twelve-year-old children (n = 259) and adults (n = 22) were presented with 36 pictures of different family constellations while their eye gaze was tracked.
