The results indicate that children below the age of three shifted from an early preference for adult faces to a preference for child faces, and they attended more to male than female adults. Adults between 20 and 30 years of age shifted from no preference to a preference for faces of young children. Older children did not show a preference for any particular demographic. Thus, across childhood, social interests change, potentially explained by a person’s physical needs and interests.

articles.title: The Repeatable Social Stress Test (ReSST): a guide and validation of a novel paradigm to elicit repeatable stress responses in humans
articles.authors: Cecilia Vezzani; Liva Martinussen; Matthew Thompson; Claudia Pazmandi; Vera Rudi; Nasimeh Naseri; Martin Trøstheim; Molly Carlyle; Isabell M. Meier; Guro Engvig Løseth
articles.abstract: Stress induction tasks have been widely used to understand human stress mechanisms, yet are limited for assessing repeated or extended stress events, especially within-subject changes. Here, we provide a guide for implementation of the Repeatable Social Stress Test (ReSST), accompanied by validation results in healthy volunteers. The ReSST is developed to induce repeated stress responses both within and across sessions in a hybrid format, consisting of adaptions of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) and the Iowa Singing Social Stress Test (I-SSST) and two novel, closely matched no-stress control conditions. Video recordings designed to remind participants of the social-evaluative component of the stress induction are used for repeating stress within sessions. The ReSST was validated in 66 healthy volunteers aged 19-58 who completed 4 sessions (2 stress, 2 control). Compared to controls, both stress induction conditions elicited comparable, robust increases in subjective stress, heart rate, and cortisol, as well as marked changes in affect. Sex differences emerged, with women exhibiting stronger subjective responses. Cortisol responses did not significantly differ by sex. Stress reminders successfully evoked subjective and physiological responses within sessions, demonstrating reliable stress reactivation beyond the initial induction. In sum, the ReSST provides researchers with a validated, repeatable tool for inducing robust stress responses within and across sessions, enabling study of recurring stress in experimental settings. To accompany our guide, we provide a detailed step-by-step protocol and materials’ overview shared on OSF. Finally, we reflect on our experiences designing and implementing the ReSST in the context of broader literature.

articles.title: Developing a measure for the need for sex
articles.authors: Oliver C. Schultheiss; Jessica Hinzmann
articles.abstract: The chapter “Developing a measure of the need for sex” presents results from a research program that aimed at developing a picture-story measure of the need for sex (n Sex) through an experimental-manipulation, measure, indicator, and criterion (EMMIC) validation approach. The resulting coding system, which also includes a measure of sexual conflict, is comprised of categories that were reliably sensitive to motive arousal across 6 studies with more than 800 participants. Findings demonstrating the measure’s validity in terms of associations with affective processes accompanying experimental motive arousal and in terms of predicting a behavioral outcome are presented. Results documenting n Sex’s convergent and discriminant validity with other implicit and explicit motive measures and with participant gender are also reported.

articles.title: Investigating prospective associations between household food insecurity and eating disorder pathology in young people in the UK: Evidence from Understanding Society
articles.authors: Akansha Naraindas; Francesca Solmi; Vivienne Hazzard; Fidan Turk
articles.abstract: Adolescence is a critical developmental period for the emergence of eating disorders, and the rising prevalence of food insecurity in the UK, particularly among families with children, raises important questions about whether this may contribute to the development of eating disorder pathology. Despite evidence linking food insecurity to eating disorder risk, adolescents remain underrepresented in this literature. This study investigates prospective associations of household food insecurity with dieting/weight loss behaviours and negative appearance evaluations in a UK cohort of adolescents. The study uses data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (Waves 13 (2021-2023) and 15 (2023-2025)). Household food insecurity was assessed at Wave 13, while dieting/weight-loss behaviours and appearance evaluations were assessed among adolescents in Wave 15. Associations were investigated using univariable and multivariable modified Poisson (for dieting/weight loss behaviours) and linear (for appearance concerns) regression models controlling for socio-demographics, main carer mental health, ethnicity, financial strain, and urban/rural residence. The analytical sample included 1140 participants (52% female, 18.8% ethnic minority). In the fully adjusted model, there was a weak association between household food insecurity and later dieting/weight loss behaviours in adolescents (risk ratio = 1.07, 95% CI: 0.99 – 1.16). There was no evidence that greater food insecurity was associated with increased appearance concerns in adolescents in any models.  While reducing food insecurity should remain a public health priority, the present findings provide weak evidence that food insecurity represents a risk factor for dieting/weight loss behaviours among UK adolescents, and no evidence that it is associated with later appearance concerns.

articles.title: The Joint Effects of Measurement Error and Model Misspecification on Statistical Interactions
articles.authors: Aljoscha Rimpler; Henk Kiers; Don van Ravenzwaaij
articles.abstract: Measurement error in predictors and unmodelled interaction effects pose recurring challenges in psychological research, yet their joint consequences for regression analysis have not been analytically characterized. We show that classical measurement error and the omission of a true interaction effect are not independent sources of bias, but become entangled such that their combined effects cannot be recovered by applying standard corrections for either problem alone. Specifically, we derive closed-form expressions for the probability limits of OLS regression weights under joint measurement error and interaction omission, characterize the implied asymptotic residual structure, and establish expressions for model fit and prediction error for infinite samples. A key finding is that the residual contributions from measurement error and interaction omission can partially cancel each other out, so that prediction error reduces marginally while leaving coefficient bias large. As a consequence, qualitatively different models can become difficult to distinguish by standard fit metrics, even in large samples. Furthermore, we demonstrate via Monte Carlo simulation that models with more biased estimates can exhibit lower estimator variance, meaning misspecified models may dominate in both inferential and model selection procedures. These results have direct implications for the replicability and interpretability of linear regression models in psychological research.

articles.title: Interictal Epileptiform Discharges and Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcomes in Children with Early-Onset Epilepsy: A Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis
articles.authors: Uffaq Mastoor; Iva Peh; Jemima Alston; Emily Lamcastle; Javier Escudero; Catherine J Crompton; Jayakara Shetty
articles.abstract:
Background: Children with early-onset epilepsy (seizure onset ≤ 5 years) are at elevated risk of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, including cognitive impairment, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum features. Seizure burden alone provides limited prognostic information. Interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs), spike or sharp-wave complexes occurring between clinical seizures on electroencephalography (EEG), are common in paediatric epilepsy and may reflect brain network instability relevant to neurodevelopment. Whether interictal EEG features recorded in early childhood are associated with long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes remains unclear.
Methods: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with a prospectively registered protocol (PROSPERO: CRD420251162420) and reported per PRISMA 2020 guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, PsycINFO, and Scopus were searched from 1966 to October 2025. Longitudinal studies examining interictal EEG features in children with epilepsy onset ≤ 5 years, with neurodevelopmental outcomes assessed ≥12 months after baseline EEG, were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using QUIPS; certainty of evidence using GRADE.
Results: Of 1,613 records identified, four longitudinal studies met inclusion criteria (epilepsy contexts: infant-onset focal epilepsy, Sturge–Weber syndrome, epileptic encephalopathies, cryptogenic generalised epilepsies). Across all four studies, greater severity or disruption of interictal EEG activity showed a directional association with poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes. All four studies were rated at moderate to high risk of bias. Certainty of evidence was low to very low across all outcome domains.
Conclusions: Directional evidence links interictal EEG severity to neurodevelopmental outcomes in early-onset epilepsy. However, the evidence base is too sparse, insufficiently standardised, and of too low methodological quality to support definitive prognostic inference. Standardised, state-resolved IED metrics and harmonised outcome batteries are needed to clarify the prognostic role of interictal activity in early-onset epilepsy.
Keywords: epilepsy; interictal epileptiform discharges; electroencephalography; prognosis; neurodevelopment; cognition; paediatric

articles.title: Sensory Processing Sensitivity is associated with Heightened Emotional Response, not Rumination when viewing Climate‑Change Media Content
articles.authors: Annalisa Setti; Catherine Trearty; Anna Oberhaeusser; Anna O'Brien
articles.abstract: Climate change is becoming increasingly recognised as a serious determinant of mental health, with indirect exposure via climate related media eliciting emotional distress and rumination. The present study sought to explore whether sensory processing sensitivity (SPS) moderates responses to climate-related videos, due to higher empathy and depth of processing characterising highly sensitive individuals. In a pre-post experimental design, 119 participants were randomly assigned to view either a climate disaster video or a control weather forecast. Positive affect, negative affect, and rumination were assessed before and after exposure. Results indicated that exposure to climate-related content significantly increased negative affect. SPS moderated this effect, such that individuals higher in sensitivity showed greater increases in negative affect in the climate condition. Nature connectedness also emerged as a significant positive predictor of negative affect, whereas climate change anxiety did not significantly predict outcomes in the final models. Positive affect and rumination were primarily explained by baseline levels and were not significantly influenced by condition or SPS. These findings suggest that negatively valenced climate-related media may elicit distress-related emotional responses, particularly among individuals high in sensory sensitivity, indicating that this dimension is of relevance when studying distressing nature-related situations.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Reliance on Generative AI in Schoolwork: The Role of Executive Functioning Difficulties, Perceived Usefulness, and Habitual Use
articles.authors: Johan Klarin; Eva Hoff; Daiva Daukantaite
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are becoming an increasingly common part of adolescents’ everyday and academic life, raising important questions about which individuals may be more likely to rely on them when facing challenges. Drawing on theories of technology adoption, habit formation, and self-regulation, the present study examined a sequential mediation model linking executive functioning (EF) difficulties to reliance on GenAI, defined as a tendency to depend on GenAI rather than one’s own effort or teacher support when encountering academic challenges, through perceived usefulness and habitual use. The model was tested using structural equation modeling in community samples of lower secondary school students (N = 849, Mage = 14.8 years, 49.4% girls) and upper secondary school students (N = 898, Mage = 17.4 years, 55.2% girls). Across both groups, EF difficulties were positively associated with perceived usefulness, habitual use, and reliance on GenAI (rs = .14–.32, ps < .001). Supporting the hypothesized model, the sequential indirect pathway through perceived usefulness and habitual use was significant in both groups (βs = .08–.10, ps < .001). Perceived usefulness emerged as the most consistent mediator, whereas habitual use showed a more limited mediating role despite being strongly associated with reliance (βs = .60–.69, ps < .001). The findings identify EF as an important individual-difference correlate of reliance on GenAI and suggest that perceived usefulness may be a key mechanism linking EF difficulties to reliance. More broadly, the results highlight the role of self-regulatory capacities in adolescents’ reliance on GenAI.

articles.title: Handing over control: A longitudinal study of delegation and disclosure in human-AI interaction
articles.authors: Teresa Luther; Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle; Angelica Lermann Henestrosa
articles.abstract: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into everyday tasks raises important questions about how individuals rely on these systems in the long run. While prior research has primarily examined cross-sectional predictors of AI use, little is known about how willingness to delegate tasks and disclose information to AI develops over time. The present study addresses this gap examining a six-wave longitudinal survey (N = 1,008 at baseline) conducted over ten months with a U.S. sample. We investigated changes in willingness to delegate professional and personal writing tasks to AI, as well as willingness to disclose information to AI, and tested the influence of user-related (experience, frequency of use, attitudes, and knowledge) and AI-related evaluative factors (trust, anthropomorphism, social actor perception). Contrary to expectations, willingness to delegate and disclose decreased over time, with the decline attenuating across waves. Willingness to delegate remained consistently higher for professional than for personal tasks. Use frequency, positive attitudes, trust, and anthropomorphism were associated with greater willingness to delegate, whereas experience and social actor perception showed no consistent effects. Willingness to disclose was similarly shaped by use and attitudinal factors. These findings suggest that human-AI interaction reflects a process of calibration rather than increasing reliance, highlighting the importance of temporal dynamics in understanding AI adoption and use.

articles.title: No Escape from Behavior in Evaluating Compositionality
articles.authors: Najoung Kim
articles.abstract: Evaluating whether a natural or artificial system exhibits compositionality is an empirical problem of active interest in both Cognitive Science and Artificial Intelligence. Because any function admits some compositional analysis, we need theoretical commitments that clearly define the target function for the question to be well-formed. Which function is appropriate depends on one's domain and scope of inquiry, and no single function is inherently privileged without further independent commitments; the only plausibly universal constraint is that the domain must admit at least one primitive-reuse analysis. Given a properly operationalized notion of compositionality, I argue that there is no escape from behavior in asking whether a system exhibits compositionality. From a constitutive perspective, the complete functional profile is sufficient for the verdict. From an empirical perspective, targeted generalization behavior over withheld recombinations is the critical evidence supporting inductive hypotheses about the function. Contra recent literature arguing that the compositionality verdict should be grounded in mechanistic evidence, mechanism is neither a necessary nor a sufficient adjudicator because it is constitutively subordinate to or evidentially dependent on behavior. Instead, the role of mechanistic evidence is best understood as a bootstrap to the inductive process and an aid to the characterization of the target function. Furthermore, settling the _is-compositional_ question rigorously opens up ways for genuine questions _about_ the mechanism and the behavior-mechanism interface to proceed productively. Finally, this discussion highlights that the critical bottleneck for the _is-compositional_ verdict on contemporary systems is data transparency rather than interpretability.

articles.title: Smoking Exposure Application (SEA): Development and Validation of An Augmented Reality Smoking Cessation App
articles.authors: Reza Barzegar; Javad hatami; Peyman Ghobadi-Azbari; Hamed Ekhtiari; Tara Rezapour
articles.abstract:
Background: Cue-reactivity is a cornerstone of addiction research; however, laboratory-based investigations often lack ecological validity, failing to generalize to real-world experiences. Augmented reality (AR) technology offers a promising solution by bridging the gap between laboratory settings and real-life environments for cue-exposure interventions. 
Objectives: The present study aimed to: (1) develop and validate a set of three-dimensional (3D) smoking-related objects through user evaluation among smokers; and (2) to incorporate these validated images into a smoking cessation application, the Smoking Exposure Application (SEA), designed to elicit cravings within familiar contexts without physical cigarette exposure.
Method: We developed 21 3D objects, including 10 smoking-related cues (e.g., cigarette, ashtray) and 11 control objects (e.g., pencil, gum pack). Forty-five participants (21 smokers and 24 non-smokers) evaluated the objects using the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) to rate valence, arousal, dominance, and desire to smoke. Additionally, participants assessed SEA’s naturalness and integration, and perceived object presence using a 0–10 scale, alongside qualitative comments.
Results: Within-group analysis showed that smokers reported significantly higher ratings for smoking-related objects compared to control objects across valence, arousal, dominance, and desire to smoke (p < 0.001). Conversely, non-smokers rated control objects higher than smoking-related objects in valence and arousal. Between-group analysis confirmed that smokers reported significantly higher responses to smoking-related objects than non-smokers, particularly regarding desire to smoke (p < 0.001). 
Conclusions: The 3D dataset effectively elicited smoking craving and associated emotional and regulatory responses (valence, arousal, and dominance) in smokers. The SEA provided an immersive and ecologically valid experience, supporting its potential utility as a digital tool for smoking cue-exposure interventions.

articles.title: An Individual-Level Paradigm for Research on Deception Cues: An Urgent Proposal
articles.authors: Erik Mac Giolla; Timothy John Luke
articles.abstract: All psychological theories of deception cues concern explanatory mechanisms at the level of the individual. However, past research on deception cues compares the behavior of truth tellers and liars at the group level. Unless two conditions are met, that the statistical models do not vary (i) across individuals or (ii) across occasions in time, group-level findings cannot accurately describe the behavior of individuals. We show that these conditions are unlikely to hold for deception cues. This means the current group-level research cannot provide a meaningful test of the individual-level mechanisms key to understanding deception cues. In order to draw meaningful conclusions about these individual-level mechanisms, the field needs a wholly different research paradigm, based on repeated measures designs. We outline a proposal for such an individual-level research agenda. Without this development, fundamental questions in deception research will remain unanswered and theories of deception will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Revisiting the Blind Implantation Paradigm: Robustness of False Memory Induction Under Controlled Conditions
articles.authors: Elsa Gewehr; Sarah Viertel; Henry Otgaar; Kristin Jankowsky
articles.abstract: The Blind Implantation paradigm was introduced as a scalable method for inducing false autobiographical memories without human interaction (Otgaar et al., 2022). We conducted a conceptual replication (N = 348) with a sample three times the size of the original, using a multi-target event design and a non-suggestive control group. Results confirm that the procedure reliably induces false beliefs and memories, supporting the reconstructive nature of memory. However, induction rates (12–15% for beliefs; 8.5% for memories) were substantially lower than in the original study. Furthermore, we found no evidence of an imagination effect, likely attributable to low task compliance. Exploratory analyses of written accounts support the validity of the paradigm and the utilized self-report scales. We discuss the implications for the scalability of memory research, emphasizing the need for comprehensive construct validation to assure differentiation of genuine memory distortion from other experimental effects in unmonitored online settings.

articles.title: Foundations of English as a Foreign Language Literacy: Cognitive and Linguistic Contributions to English Reading and Spelling in Young German Learners
articles.authors: Heike Mlakar; Benjamin Goecke
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This longitudinal study investigated the cognitive and linguistic predictors of English as a foreign language (EFL) literacy among elementary school children in Germany, focusing on reading comprehension, pseudoword reading, reading fluency, and real-word and pseudoword spelling.

Method: A sample of 107 students (53 boys, 54 girls; M_age = 10.52, SD = 0.64; 82 L1 German, 25 with other L1) was assessed at the beginning of Grade 3 on cognitive abilities (phonological awareness, phonological short-term memory, working memory, nonverbal intelligence) and linguistic skills (English vocabulary and grammar). Linear mixed-effects models, including age, gender, and language background as covariates, were used to predict six EFL literacy outcomes at the end of Grade 4, accounting for the nested data structure.

Results: Nonverbal intelligence and phonological awareness were robust predictors of EFL reading comprehension, with L2 vocabulary adding a further contribution. Beyond comprehension, distinct skills predicted distinct outcomes: phonological short-term memory predicted pseudoword reading, L2 receptive grammar and vocabulary predicted real-word spelling, and nonverbal intelligence predicted pseudoword spelling. These additional effects align with theoretical models and offer encouraging initial evidence that merits replication. Reading fluency was not predicted by the variables examined. 

Conclusion: The findings underscore the necessity of fostering vocabulary, grammatical knowledge, and phonological processing, alongside general cognitive skills, in EFL literacy instruction for young learners. Adopting a multidimensional perspective can inform targeted literacy support strategies and offer a better understanding of the knowledge bases underlying early EFL literacy in non-English-speaking contexts.

articles.title: Overall attitudes towards quantum computing are more positive than overall attitudes towards artificial intelligence considering also knowledge levels
articles.authors: Christian Montag; Rostam J. Neuwirth; Magnus Liebherr
articles.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a major topic of public and scientific debate, whereas public perceptions of quantum computing (QC) remain less understood. In the present study, we aimed to understand if people have different views on AI vs. QC, while also asking them about their perceived knowledge levels in these two domains. Further, we investigated the construct of technology self-efficacy to consider how people in general think they can master new technology. 
In N = 475 German speaking participants from the general population (227 females, 248 males) we observed a) that people report on average more positive attitudes towards QC than towards AI, while b) at the same time reporting less knowledge on QC compared to AI. In mediation models, we observed that the link between technology self-efficacy and more positive AI / QC attitudes is mediated by knowledge levels about AI / QC. We also shed light on further mediation models with negative AI / QC attitudes and pessimism aversion in the context of AI / QC as outcomes. 
The present data could be interpreted in a way that the massive global discussions on AI technology might make people less positive towards this general-purpose technology compared to overall QC attitudes, whereas interestingly the reported knowledge levels about QC are lower than those regarding AI. This is noteworthy, as it is discussed that the fusion of QC and AI technology will represent a powerful merger likely leading to a dramatic increase of scientific discovery, an assumption that received moderate support in the present sample.

articles.title: Obsessive Thinking About a Loved One in Romantic Love: Eight Perspectives
articles.authors: Adam Bode; Sandra Langeslag
articles.abstract: Obsessive thinking about a loved one (i.e., constant, involuntary, repetitive thoughts about the loved one) is a defining feature of romantic love yet remains markedly under-researched. This article provides the first review of obsessive thinking about a loved one in romantic love, organising the disparate literature using an "Eight Perspectives" approach spanning evolutionary history, evolutionary functions, development, mechanisms, ecology, cognitions, emotions, and behaviour. We argue that obsessive thinking about a loved one likely emerged by co-opting mother-infant bonding circuitry, appears across cultures and across the lifespan, and may have evolved to promote proximity-seeking and sustained orientation toward a loved one. Contrary to long-standing claims, the mechanisms underlying obsessive thinking in romantic love are unlikely to be shared with obsessive-compulsive disorder. People who are in love think about their loved one for approximately 50% of their waking hours, and this thinking is associated with romantic (but not companionate) love, distraction, proximity-seeking behaviour, and analgesia. Whether such thinking is experienced as bothersome or enjoyable depends less on its frequency than on companionate love and reciprocation. We conclude by identifying priorities for future research across all eight perspectives.

articles.title: Subjective and physiological measures reveal emotionally salient moments in virtual everyday life
articles.authors: Ruhoollah Akhundzadeh; Johanna Hokka; Mikko Sams; Eeva Puumala; Heini Saarimäki
articles.abstract:
Emotions in everyday life are dynamic, context-dependent, and socially embedded, yet most psychophysiological research relies on highly controlled and often artificial laboratory paradigms. This raises questions about whether emotional processes observed under such conditions generalize to naturalistic contexts and how subjective and physiological measures relate in everyday settings.

The present study addresses these challenges by combining ethnographically informed virtual reality (VR) stimuli with multimodal measurement of emotional responses. Participants viewed immersive 360° videos depicting everyday social encounters while electrocardiography, skin conductance, facial electromyography, and gaze patterns were recorded. Following each scenario, participants provided affective ratings across multiple dimensions, including valence, arousal, approach–avoidance, and social connectedness.

Across measures, results revealed systematic but context-dependent divergence between subjective and physiological responses. Associations between modalities were generally weak and selective rather than reflecting consistent one-to-one correspondence. Instead, different measures appeared to capture complementary aspects of emotional processing. Furthermore, relationships between physiological signals and affective ratings varied across events, highlighting the role of contextual and social meaning in shaping emotional responses.

These findings suggest that emotional experience in everyday contexts cannot be reduced to single physiological or subjective indicators but is better understood as a multi-component, context-sensitive process. The results underscore the importance of multimodal approaches and ecologically valid designs. More broadly, they demonstrate the potential of immersive VR as a methodological framework for studying naturalistic emotional experiences while maintaining experimental control.

articles.title: Development, Content Validation, and Preliminary Accessibility Testing of a Workplace Well-Being Assessment Tool for Workers with Intellectual Disabilities
articles.authors: Elodie Leclerc; Clément Ginoux; Pascale Leconte; Marine Peslier; Sophie Posseme; Anne Palanque; Tiphaine Huyghebaert-Zouaghi; Nolwenn Charles; Julio César Alves Da Silva; Sandrine Isoard-Gautheur
articles.abstract:
Background: Workplace well-being is a critical determinant of job retention for people with intellectual disabilities. Despite its importance, no validated instrument exists to assess this construct among these workers. The objective of the present research was therefore to develop a battery of questionnaire tailored to people with intellectual disabilities in sheltered employment to assess workplace well-being and its associated factors. Furthermore, this study aimed to provide evidence regarding the instrument's content validity and initial evidence of its accessibility for the target population.
Method: In a first study, the content of the developed questionnaire battery was evaluated by an expert committee using the Lynn method. The instrument included four indicators of workplace well-being (i.e., burnout, need for recovery, vigor, job satisfaction), job characteristics (i.e., job demands and job resources), and off-duty recovery (i.e., recovery activities and experiences), variables based on the JD-R model, DISC-R model and recovery theories. In a second study, this validated questionnaire was administered to 29 participants to assess its accessibility.
Results: All 80 items developed received content validation by the expert committee. The pilot study conducted with the target population provided initial evidence of the instrument accessibility.
Conclusion: Further research is needed to test the questionnaire with a larger sample to provide psychometric evidence and additional evidence of its accessibility for workers with intellectual disabilities.

articles.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of efficacy beliefs in pro-environmental behavior change
articles.authors: Christina M. Juchem; Karen R.S. Hamann; Susanne Buecker; Lisa Marie Warner; Saskia Baumgardt; Abira Suthakaran; Leonie C. Bandurski; Eva Asselmann
articles.abstract: Efficacy beliefs – individuals’ conviction that their actions can make a meaningful difference – are widely regarded as key psychological drivers of pro-environmental behavior and promising targets for climate interventions. Yet it remains unclear whether changing these beliefs translates into action. We conducted a preregistered systematic review synthesizing longitudinal and interventional evidence (129 studies; N ≈ 65,000) to evaluate whether, and under what conditions, efficacy beliefs promote pro-environmental behavior change. After correcting for publication bias, efficacy interventions showed no meaningful effect on intention and behavior (d = 0.01-0.04), largely because most interventions failed to reliably increase efficacy beliefs. Multi-session interventions showed greater promise, whereas brief, message-based interventions were ineffective in altering pro-environmental action. These findings challenge assumptions about the malleability and behavioral impact of efficacy beliefs and redirect research toward understanding how efficacy beliefs can be durably strengthened and interact with social and structural factors to promote climate action.

articles.title: Whole-brain anatomical and temporal patterns  hypothesized to be evoked during a false-belief fMRI task
articles.authors: Konrad F. Jennicke; Ava Momeni; Maddie Evora; Todd Stephen Woodward
articles.abstract:
Background: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) investigations of theory of 
mind and false-belief processing have been central to cognitive neuroscience for several 
decades. Drawing on previous fMRI studies, we (1) hypothesize that a task-general brain 
mode (DMB) will emerge during the false-belief task, (2) specify its anatomical properties, 
and (3) hypothesize how it will respond, in terms of blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) 
signal changes, to task conditions in a false-belief task.
Task: The false-belief task involved story processing involving either theory of mind or only 
physical properties, resulting in two conditions: (1) Mental, and (2) Physical.
Anatomical: The spatial patterns for Default Mode B (DMB; Lemon, Headlights, Flying 
Seagull, Tripod and Angel Wings) are provided in Figure 1.
Temporal: DMB is predicted to activate during the Mental condition due to engagement of 
theory of mind processes, and to deactivate during the Physical condition. Both are predicted 
to involve a mid-trial peak activation or deactivation. Details are presented in the text below 
and Figure 3.
Analysis: Constrained Principal Component Analysis for fMRI (fMRI-CPCA), an 
application of multivariate multiple regression with a finite impulse response model of the 
task timing, followed by dimensionality reduction, will be used to test these hypotheses.
Conclusions: For the false-belief task, DMB is hypothesized to emerge and show specific 
spatial and temporal characteristics. Although examined within the context of false-belief 
tasks, this mode is not specific to this task. Rather, it is part of a broader set of task-general 
functional brain modes observed across multiple cognitive tasks. This approach may provide 
insight into cognitive processes detectable by fMRI underlying theory of mind.

articles.title: Minimum Cost Psychological Defense: Theoretical Construction and Anti-Fraud Application
articles.authors: Lijie Zhou; Yifan Zhou; Zihuan Pei
articles.abstract: Human decision-making under acute stress reveals a critical paradox in applied social psychology: despite possessing adequate declarative risk knowledge, individuals frequently exhibit a knowing-doing gap when confronting high-pressure digital deception. Traditional interventions demanding substantial cognitive resources often fail when deceivers hijack victims' limited cognitive bandwidth via emotional manipulation. To address this, we propose the Minimum Cost Psychological Defense (M.C.P.D.) model. In Study 1, using a mixed-methods design (N = 679), we developed and validated the Public Anti-Fraud Skill Scale. It comprises three dimensions—emotional buffering, proactive defense, and distributed help-seeking—which significantly predicted reduced real-world victimization risk. In Study 2, a double-blind randomized controlled trial (N = 185) evaluated an emergency guide that encodes complex verification tasks into simple implementation intentions. Compared to traditional education, this micro-skill intervention significantly reduced compliance impulses under simulated high-pressure fraud scenarios and shortened decision-making response times, indicating successful cognitive offloading. By transforming declarative knowledge into procedural, automated micro-skills, the M.C.P.D. strategy effectively bypasses executive function limitations. This shifts the anti-fraud paradigm from trait assessment to dynamic behavioral blocking, providing significant contributions to dual-process theory and a scalable tool for practical interventions.

articles.title: Realistic deepfakes are detected better from a single glance than deliberate inspection
articles.authors: Dalia Israel; Timothy Cottier; Genevieve Quek; Manuel Varlet; Tijl Grootswagers
articles.abstract: The rapidly increasing realism of AI-generated faces threatens trust in digital media, as observers often fail to reliably distinguish AI-generated faces from real faces under prolonged viewing. Across three experiments, participants (N = 300) classified faces varying in realism, exposure duration, and feature availability as real or AI-generated. Observers detected AI-generated faces above chance based on 83 ms when external features, such as hair and background, were present, whereas unlimited viewing did not improve detection of realistic AI-generated faces. These findings suggest observers can extract gist-based authenticity-related signals from a single glimpse, but these may be overridden during prolonged evaluative face processing.

articles.title: Acoustic and social bonding differences between Japanese singing and conversation: A Registered Report replicating Ozaki et al. (2024)
articles.authors: Gakuto Chiba; Yuto Ozaki; Shinya Fujii; Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: Understanding cross-cultural differences between singing and speech is a central goal of the Many Voices project (Savage et al. 2025a). As part of this effort, the present study examined Japanese participants (n=10 for confirmatory acoustic analysis; 15 for exploratory behavioural analysis) singing the traditional folk song Tokyo Ondo or having a conversation about favourite foods. Confirmatory analyses replicated previously reported tendencies (Ozaki et al., 2024): singing was higher in pitch, slower in temporal rate, and used more stable pitches than spoken conversation. Temporal rate showed a large effect (Cohen’s d = 1.6), while pitch height (d = 0.55) and pitch stability (d = 0.39) showed medium effect sizes. Exploratory analyses of relationships between acoustic features and social variables suggested that singing increased participants’ self-reported sense of social bonding, and individuals reporting higher perceived synchrony tended to show greater singing–speech differences. This study provides culturally grounded data of Japanese conversation and traditional singing for cross-cultural vocal research and underscores the importance of including traditional repertoires in studies of acoustic variation. The Many Voices project will continue collecting data from up to 24 additional languages and regions, with a subsequent meta-analysis assessing cross-linguistic consistency in singing–speech differences.

articles.title: Synthetic digital content as a research tool in Social Sciences: From deepfakes to responsible synthetic digital content creation
articles.authors: Michal Mochtak; Joep van Lit
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is frequently viewed through the lens of “deepfakes” and the risks of deception. This paper argues that such a framing obscures the potential of synthetic media as a rigorous research tool in the social sciences. We propose the neutral term “synthetic digital content” (SDC) and establish a framework for its responsible use based on three pillars: ethicality, methodological rigor, and researcher accountability. To maintain these standards, we advocate for a “do-it-yourself” (DIY) approach using open-source models rather than proprietary closed-system alternatives. We provide a practical roadmap for SDC production focusing on incorporating legal frameworks, ethical safeguards, and technical “recipes” and demonstrate its feasibility through an illustrative case study. By offering clear benchmarks for both the creation and evaluation of SDC, this paper provides a pragmatic guide for researchers, reviewers, and readers to leverage synthetic digital content in social science research while mitigating ethical and technical risks.

articles.title: How Sovereign Control, Decarbonization, and Energy Costs Shape Public Support for Data Centers
articles.authors: Jonas Heering; Erik Voeten
articles.abstract: The rapid expansion of data centers has created new political challenges. Governments want to build more data centers within their borders to reap the benefits from the artificial intelligence (AI) economy and achieve their digital sovereignty agendas. However, data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and water, threaten emission-reduction targets, and often raise electricity prices. As a result, local communities increasingly mobilize against data center construction. We use a vignette and conjoint survey experiment in Germany to evaluate how publics think about the environmental, economic, and (geo)political tradeoffs that data centers entail. We find that directly priming people with digital sovereignty concerns only marginally increases support for building more data centers. Yet, support for data centers varies substantially based on characteristics that people do have strong views about: decarbonization, geopolitics, and local environmental and economic impact. Geopolitical concerns are particularly salient: people strongly favor data centers operated by German or European firms over US or Chinese operators. These effects are large even when compared to the effects of substantial electricity price increases and variation in energy sources. Our findings suggest that public opposition over data centers depends on pre-existing political cleavages and that sovereignty concerns loom large.

articles.title: Local Roots as Door Openers: The Rise of the Far Right in Rural Communities
articles.authors: Thomas Tichelbaecker
articles.abstract: How do new far-right parties establish themselves in local communities despite lacking an established reputation and facing political stigmatization? This article argues that local candidates help overcome these barriers through two distinct mechanisms. Candidates with high socioeconomic status (SES) provide informational cues about competence and legitimacy, whereas locally rooted candidates mobilize interpersonal networks within local communities. I test these arguments using a novel dataset covering 455,817 candidacies in 1,362 county elections in Germany, linked to candidate characteristics and individual electoral performance. Exploiting open-list electoral rules, I show that both high-SES and locally rooted candidates receive an electoral bonus, but that these advantages are substantially larger for candidates of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) than for candidates of other parties. The electoral advantage of locally rooted AfD candidates is particularly pronounced in rural counties. To distinguish between network mobilization and cue-based mechanisms, I estimate candidates’ hometown advantage using individual-level vote returns. Whereas high-SES AfD candidates do not perform disproportionately well in their hometowns, locally rooted AfD candidates do, consistent with the mobilization of local interpersonal networks. Additional analyses indicate that the advantage of high-SES candidates increases where high-SES competitors are more common, while the local-roots advantage appears specific to the AfD rather than a general feature of new parties. The findings demonstrate that locally embedded elites play a distinctive role in facilitating the local breakthrough of new far-right parties and highlight the importance of interpersonal networks in explaining their electoral success.

articles.title: Demand Networks and Informal Volunteering
articles.authors: Hjalmar Bang Carlsen; Jonas Toubøl
articles.abstract: Patterns of volunteering have predominantly been explained by focusing on the supply side in terms of volunteers’ resources and motivations. We shift the focus to the demand side of volunteering and develop the concept of demand networks. We argue that experienced demand for help in one’s personal network is important to explain why individuals engage in informally organized voluntary help and support: the amount of demand for help a person experiences in their network influences the likelihood that the person helps. To explain why individuals who perceive similar levels of demand do not all volunteer to the same extent, we theorize how demand networks are mediated by the institutional factors of social values and gender roles. We hypothesize that altruistic values and gendered social roles dispose individuals to respond differently to demands for help, with women and those holding stronger altruistic values being more likely to act on the needs they perceive. We examine the hypotheses using a cross-sectional survey inquiring about informally organized volunteering during COVID-19. The results clearly indicate the importance of the demand side to adequately explain informal volunteering. We argue that our findings imply that sociologists should reconceptualize social connections not only as providing access to resources but also as a source of demands on individuals. In doing so attention should be paid to gender roles which the results suggest function as an amplifier of demand networks association with informal volunteering. We further discuss how the results have implications for building social capital and societal resilience in times of crisis.

articles.title: Publication bias inflates estimates of the effectiveness of common educational interventions
articles.authors: Bastian Andreas Betthäuser; Bartholomew Konechni; Vanessa Astrid Wittemann; Gaia Grassi; Susan Swingler; Anders Bach-Mortensen; Niklas Ayris; Una Oljaca
articles.abstract: While there is a large body of evidence on the effectiveness of educational interventions, the robustness of this evidence has not been systematically assessed. Here we conduct a preregistered systematic review, quality appraisal, and meta-analysis of all available estimates of the effects of four common supplementary learning interventions—tutoring, summer programs, afterschool programs, and extended instruction time—on children’s learning in mathematics and reading. We use multiple diagnostic techniques to assess the risk of bias of individual effect size estimates and to test for publication bias in the evidence base on supplementary learning interventions as a whole. We find that about half of all effect size estimates are at serious or critical risk of bias, with confounding and deviation from intended treatment being the most prominent risk-of-bias domains. We find substantial publication bias in the existing evidence base, indicated by a marked discontinuity in the distribution of test statistics at the conventional significance threshold and a significant association between magnitude and precision of effect size estimates. We combine five bias-correction techniques to estimate bias-adjusted effects for the four intervention types. Correcting for publication bias substantially reduces effect size estimates for tutoring, summer programs, and extended instruction time and renders estimates for afterschool programs statistically insignificant. After correction, tutoring is the only intervention that consistently yields positive and statistically significant effects. Our findings suggest that the existing evidence base substantially overestimates the effectiveness of commonly implemented supplementary learning interventions.

articles.title: The Double Bind of LGBTQ+ Inclusion in English Foster Care
articles.authors: Han Greenslade
articles.abstract: LGBTQ+ young people are likely to be overrepresented in the English care system and face disproportionately high levels of placement instability, discrimination, and poor mental health. Foster carers are expected to provide safe and affirming care but do so within a system characterised by inconsistent training, limited guidance, and increasing political contestation around gender and sexuality. This study explores how foster carers in England experience and enact LGBTQ+ inclusion through qualitative interviews with fifteen foster carers conducted in 2025. Drawing on a critical realist methodology and informed by the work of Nikolas Rose, Pierre Bourdieu, and Sara Ahmed, the analysis identifies a structural double bind at the heart of contemporary fostering. Carers are responsibilised for delivering inclusive practice while simultaneously having their relational expertise undermined by professional hierarchies and inadequate institutional support. The findings further suggest that organisational responses, including LGBTQ+ awareness training, often function as symbolic rather than enabling interventions, increasing uncertainty rather than confidence. Where affirming care occurs, it relies primarily on carers' relational commitment, experiential learning, and support from individual allies rather than coherent organisational infrastructure. The article argues that improving outcomes for LGBTQ+ young people requires structural reform that embeds LGBTQ+ inclusion within national standards, professional learning, and institutional culture.

articles.title: Reflections on educational livestreaming as a tool for teaching at scale: Some pedagogical and technological considerations
articles.authors: Lucy E Delaney
articles.abstract:
Online and hybrid courses are now a permanent fixture of the higher education landscape. Students appreciate the flexibility and convenience of such courses while institutions appreciate the potential to educate more people for less money and with fewer constraints. The question for educators remains: what are the ethics and best practices for teaching in the digital realm? And, is it possible for remote instruction to provide students with the same or similar benefits to those of in-person courses? Here I argue that when lecture-based courses expand beyond 250+ students, the potential benefits of in-person instructional activities are often limited or lost entirely. Thus as one promising solution, I outline several practical and pedagogical reasons to conduct the large-enrollment lecture within a fully online medium.

This working paper attempts to formalize a general approach to online lecturing (the "livestream model") that leverages popular and contemporary digital media tools to facilitate high-quality online education and community building at scale. The model may be used in fully online courses or ideally as part of a "blended" modality that includes a mix of synchronous instructional activities conducted either fully in person or fully online---providing students with varied and flexible opportunities for learning. In contrast to the pandemic-style "Zoom" teaching typical of synchronous online instruction, livestreaming is characterized by the use of professional audiovisual equipment and a reliance on specialized software to produce high-quality broadcasts, in addition to sustained and real-time interaction via text-based chat. Livestreaming today is one of the most popular and interactive modes of digital media consumption by Gen Z internet users. When coupled with additional instructional activities and communication tools for digital community building (e.g., Discord), the large-enrollment instructor can create a warm and personalized virtual classroom with a shared culture between hundreds of learners.

articles.title: Deservingness and solidarity activism
articles.authors: Eva Fernández G.; Jonas Toubøl
articles.abstract: Deservingness towards groups who are in need has predominantly been studied in relation to public support for welfare policies, but we argue that that deservingness is also a likely candidate for explaining participation in activism in solidarity with others. This study compares deservingness’ association with solidarity activism towards three disadvantaged groups: people without employment, people with disabilities, and refugees. Drawing on a sample of 16,916 survey respondents from Denmark, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Poland, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, we examine and compare the associations between participating in solidarity activism and perceptions of deservingness towards people without employment, with disabilities and refugees, respectively. The results confirm that deservingness is a factor strongly associated with participation in solidarity activism. Although people with disabilities are generally considered the most deserving of the three groups, deservingness plays a more decisive role in mobilizing solidarity with refugees. The results have two-fold implications for the study of solidarity activism. First, deservingness should be considered a potential driver of solidarity activism that is distinguishable from social values and shapes participation in solidarity activism following different logics across groups. Secondly, we argue that the variation in the strength of the association between deservingness and activism across the three groups can be explained in terms of the level of contention over the group’s status as deserving.

articles.title: Evaluating system-level impacts of the UK Technician Commitment: 7 years on
articles.authors: Ryan Bates; Andrew Noyes
articles.abstract: Technicians play a centrally important role in research and teaching. However, the historical low status of technical staff in institutional hierarchies presents them with a range of challenges, and has arguably hampered research and innovation. In response to this situation, the Technician Commitment was established in the UK in 2017. It encouraged signatory universities and research institutions to commit to tackling key challenges across four ‘pillars’ - visibility, recognition, career development, and sustainability. The programme has now expanded internationally, growing from 37 to 112 signatories. In this paper, we interrogate the best available administrative datasets in order to assess the impact of the Technician Commitment. The Higher Education Statistics Agency’s staff record spanning 2012/13 to 2022/23 is used to evaluate whether any system-level changes accruing from the wide-scale uptake of the Technician Commitment can be identified. Using a provisional theory of change logic model, and operationalising the four pillars into workable evaluation measures, one key change is identified. There has been an increase in the number of technicians in senior roles in signatory institutions, which is a necessary for the leadership of strategic planning and for implementation. We discuss whether this is what would have been expected at this time in the Commitment’s maturation and given the theory of change. We also compare these findings with earlier UK national system-change programmes - the Athena Swan and Race Equality charters - and their evaluations, discussing the challenges of enacting systemic change in the complex higher education sector.

articles.title: How first-time mothers bundle work and safety nets
articles.authors: Hyein Kang; Rose Geoghegan; Colleen Heflin; David W. Rothwell
articles.abstract: Being a first-time mother carries substantial consequences, including financial strain, mental and physical health adjustments, and impacts on job stability and time use. Dynamics of safety net usage among first-time mothers are well-documented, but little is known about how new mothers coordinate work and public benefits together. In this research, we study population-level employment and social safety net program participation among new mothers by linking birth records in Oregon between 2016 and 2017 to wage and program enrollment data from 2014 through 2019. Following new mothers for two years before and after their childbirth, we find a significant decrease in mothers’ employment in the quarters surrounding childbirth with a corresponding surge in reliance on safety net benefits. We also find that education, marital status, and income level were key determinants of shaping work and safety net usage patterns among first-time mothers. These shifts were especially pronounced among low socioeconomic status women, who demonstrate greater responsiveness in employment and safety net utilization around the time of birth. Our findings point to the importance of integrating both work and safety net program participation and demonstrate gaps where additional work-supports and safety net engagement would promote economic security.

articles.title: Why Do Immigrant Girls Participate Less in Organized Leisure Activities? The Role of Parental Influence Across the Transition from Adolescence to Adulthood
articles.authors: Mia Stenbro Lorenzen; Frank van Tubergen; Hans-Peter Y. Qvist
articles.abstract: Research documents immigrant-native gaps in girls’ participation in organized leisure activities across Western Europe, particularly among Muslim immigrant-origin girls. While parental characteristics are often assumed to shape these gaps, less is known about which parental factors matter most and whether their influence persists into adulthood. Using German longitudinal data from CILS4EU and CILS4EU-DE, we address these questions by examining participation gaps among non-Muslim and Muslim immigrant-origin girls relative to native girls across the transition from adolescence to early adulthood, by estimating a structural equation model that distinguishes between initial parental effects in adolescence, path-dependent effects linking adolescent and adult participation, and persistent parental effects in early adulthood. Differences in parental participation and socioeconomic resources explain a substantial share of participation gaps, whereas parental gender values play no independent role. Although participation gaps narrow over time, they persist, primarily through path-dependent processes, as lower participation during adolescence is carried forward into adulthood. Persistent parental effects remain but are comparatively modest. While participation gaps are larger among Muslim immigrant-origin girls, the underlying mechanisms are broadly similar across immigrant-origin groups. The findings highlight how family-based inequalities shape participation trajectories and contribute to the production and reproduction of participation gaps across the life course.

articles.title: Categorized Continuous Regressors and Interpretational Bias  under Covariate Adjustment
articles.authors: Gordey Yastrebov
articles.abstract: Empirical researchers often replace continuous or finely graded regressors with coarse categories to allow flexible comparisons. This paper shows that such categories can create an overlooked problem when coefficients are compared across differently adjusted models. A category coefficient represents a contrast in the underlying continuous variable, and that contrast need not remain invariant once covariates are added. When the underlying variable is related to the adjustment set, residual variation in category membership may come from a different part of the continuous distribution than the marginal category contrast. As a result, coefficients on the same category indicators can change across specifications even when added covariates have no direct role in the continuous-scale outcome process. I call this problem category non-equivalence. I formalize the mechanism, use simulations to show how it varies with covariate predictive power and category coarseness, and illustrate it empirically with maternal age at birth in the Generations and Gender Survey. The paper concludes with practical recommendations for assessing non-equivalence and interpreting coefficient changes.

articles.title: Open science in Communication: How are we doing?
articles.authors: Tobias Dienlin
articles.abstract: Communication has recently started a conversation on open science. In this narrative overview, I share perspectives on how the field of Communication is doing regarding the implementation of open science practices and principles, highlighting positive examples and suggesting missed opportunities. I discuss this process using the open science – science reform wheel, which differentiates 10 different principles and practices: transparency, accessible publishing, research process, research practices, public discourse, inclusion, research infrastructures, publication system, incentivization, and teaching and training. Although overall levels are still low, Communication has made substantial progress in terms of data sharing and preregistration. On the other hand, still no ICA journal has introduced the publication format of registered reports, which is a missed opportunity to reduce publication bias and to improve research quality.

articles.title: Describing and Predicting Bored Smartphone Use: A Field Study Combining Ecological Momentary Assessments and Screenomics
articles.authors: Paulien Decorte; Heidi Vandebosch; Eline Camerman; Karolien Poels
articles.abstract: People often seek to alleviate boredom, a common negative emotion, through smartphone use. However, current literature diverges on whether smartphones effectively alleviate boredom: mood management perspectives suggest they could, while psychologists warn they may merely provide superficial relief. Before assessing the regulatory potential of smartphones for state boredom, we first need to better understand how state boredom is related to smartphone use in daily life. Capturing boredom multifacetedly through valence, arousal, fatigue, and meaning, the present study examined how state boredom precedes day-to-day smartphone use and how bored smartphone use takes shape. Three-day field data were analyzed from N=44 young adults with smartphone unlocks triggering n=607 ecological momentary assessments and continuous Screenomics smartphone use data. Participants felt substantially bored preceding smartphone use in one-third of smartphone unlocks, with bored smartphone use peaking in the late afternoon and early evening. Bayesian Multivariate Mixed Models revealed multifaceted boredom patterns influencing smartphone app, activity, and switching behaviors, demonstrating distinct bored smartphone use patterns. Overall, bored smartphone use is complex, shaped by its related correlates, highlighting the need for multifaceted approaches in studying everyday smartphone use and its regulatory potential when people feel bored.

articles.title: Unequal labour market entry during COVID-19 in Finland: Stratification by type of degree and social origin
articles.authors: Aart-Jan Riekhoff; Satu Ojala
articles.abstract: Students who graduated in the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic faced worsened conditions for labour market entry. Moreover, it is likely that the pandemic exacerbated existing inequalities in labour market entry between graduates. Using detailed Finnish administrative data and event study models, we estimate the effects of graduating during the pandemic on monthly employment statuses and earnings for a treatment group that graduated during COVID-19 compared with a control group that graduated exactly one year earlier. We differentiate between graduates of vocational education, universities of applied sciences and universities, as well as between having parents with a lower and higher educational degree. We find that the effects of the pandemic on employment and earnings were greater for graduates with a vocational degree than for those with a degree from a university (of applied sciences) but find little difference by social origin. By exploring the role of unemployment and student benefit take-up, we find that the negative employment effects of the pandemic on vocational graduates can be partly explained by a “discouraged worker effect”, in the form of graduates continuing or re-entering education. Jobless university graduates with highly educated parents were possibly holding out longer for better jobs using unemployment benefits.

articles.title: Acts of moral courage among civil servants under democratic backsliding: A comparison of the Trump and Bolsonaro administrations
articles.authors: Jaime Kucinskas; Mariana Costa Silveira
articles.abstract: Under the administrations of U.S. President Donald J. Trump (2017–2021) and Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro (2019–2022), democratic backsliding intensified through illiberal reforms, institutional erosion, and growing political pressures on public administration. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 82 Brazilian and 66 U.S. career civil servants, this study examines episodes of moral courage, defined as principled actions rooted in higher order democratic and professional standards taken in the face of political pressure and personal risk. We find some distinctive trajectories of morally courageous actions across countries and identify the organizational and individual conditions that enable such acts. Crucially, comparable pressures did not produce comparable responses: Brazilian civil servants mobilized through more collective, open, and confrontational acts, whereas their U.S. counterparts adopted more individualized and cautious strategies. We argue that certain relational and organizational contextual factors explain this divergence.  We also identified some key factors in both countries that enabled morally courageous action. At the organizational level, supportive professional cultures and strong internal and external networks emerge as key facilitators. At the individual level, moral courage is associated with commitment to agency missions, a sense of self-efficacy, long-term moral reflection, and civic engagement. Our study contributes a cross-national comparative perspective on bureaucratic responses to democratic erosion and a conceptual framework to guide future research on defending democratic norms under illiberal rule.

articles.title: NITR SOVEREIGN WEALTH FUNDS AND NON-DEPRECIATING INVESTMENT GROWTH
articles.authors: Timothy Kessler
articles.abstract:
Sovereign wealth funds, (SWFs) are increasingly used by diverse countries to support large-scale economic development. However, limited evidence exists regarding these national outcomes. I investigate Norway and Singapore, the only open high-income (HI) economies with SWF assets exceeding GDP. Multi-model synthetic control methods (SCMs) with negative control outcomes estimate a treatment effect of $27,716 USD, $24,126 PPP, and $15,804 USD investment (2021 GDP per capita) by Norway’s Government Pension Fund (1995-2023). SCMs estimate a structural economic output acceleration of $19,124 US$, $37,006 PPP, and $21,594 USD investment per capita in Singapore attributable to its National Investment Income (NII) SWF investment (2003-2003). GPF and NII increased gross domestic savings % of GDP 8.3%, 26.4% by ratio in Norway, and 10.24%, 25.2% by ratio in Singapore.
 I identify a specific model of SWF investment in these economies “NITR,” (National-Investment Transfer-Return”), in terms of the Solow Model. Under NITR, surplus output is withheld from automatic economic capital that would typically depreciate. A majority is transferred to SWF asset growth, while a smaller share is allocated to investment capital expansion. The greater surplus value of SWF reserves withheld from capital are used to offset net national depreciation equivalent to that created by new investment output. This mechanism produced Norway and Singapore’s unique pattern of non-asymptotic late-stage output and savings rate growth, adjusted for external trade pathways. Since sources of SWF savings are heterogenous, including mandated household savings in low-income countries, modified NITR SWFs could support output and savings growth in diverse policy environments.

articles.title: Friday Night Lights Out:  A Corpus of Radio Transmissions Broadcast by the Baltimore Police Department
articles.authors: Stephen L. Morgan; Rhiannon Miller
articles.abstract:
Friday Night Lights Out (FNLO) is a corpus of two-way radio transmissions broadcast by the Baltimore Police Department (BPD).  The corpus is a subset of a larger archive of more than 91 million radio transmissions recorded on sixteen radio receivers between 2016 and 2022.  Selected from that archive, the FNLO corpus targets a single, meaningful window:  the second hour after sunset on each Friday in 2017.

A team of undergraduate research assistants first transcribed a selection of radio transmissions.  In a second phase of work, the research assistants then cut short audio segments keyed to important words and codes spoken in the transmissions, producing a set of ground-truth examples.  The result of the effort is three linked components: 138,067 short audio recordings spanning the year, 25,893 human transcriptions of a subset of the transmissions, and 14,267 keyword clips (more than half of which correspond to radio transmissions in the set of 25,893 first-stage transcriptions). 

This document provides an explanation of recording techniques for the full archive of radio transmissions, the rationale for selecting transmissions for transcription, the transcription process itself (including the guidelines given to transcribers), the codes and conventions needed to understand the transcripts, and the 2017 policing context in which the transmissions were broadcast (a year framed by a federal consent decree, an emergent corruption scandal, and elevated violent crime).

Because the transmissions contain sensitive information about possibly identifiable individuals, the authors hope to arrange in the future for the corpus to be made available to other researchers under appropriate safeguards.  For now, it is available only to researchers at the first author’s institution by joining the research team.  This document represents a step toward providing broader access to the corpus.

articles.title: Using decomposition techniques and machine learning to investigate the determinants of socioeconomic inequalities in early childcare access
articles.authors: Laudine Carbuccia
articles.abstract: Formal early childcare has a strong equalizing potential, yet access remains socioeconomically stratified. This study examines how these socioeconomic inequalities emerge and widen across three stages of the formal early childcare access process: intention to use early childcare during pregnancy, application, and actual access during the child’s first year. Using longitudinal data on approximately 2,000 families in France, collected during pregnancy and followed one year after birth, we document a progressive widening of gaps along the access pathway. Compared with high–socioeconomic status (SES) households, low–SES households are about 18% less likely to intend to use early childcare, 25% less likely to apply, and 46% less likely to obtain access. To identify the determinants of these gaps, we combine machine learning for variable selection with decomposition analyses that quantify the contribution of observable factors at each stage across a wide range of 39 predictors. At the intention stage, most of the SES gap is accounted for by differences in observable characteristics related to resources, constraints, and available alternatives, with norms contributing little. At subsequent stages, inequalities increasingly reflect institutional barriers. The largest disparities emerge at the access stage, where spot allocation-related factors favoring higher-income, working, and earlier-applying households, and knowledge of the childcare system, account for most of the gap. Overall, the results show that socioeconomic stratification in early childcare access is closely linked to the timing and design of access processes, even in systems intended to be universal.

articles.title: The Electoral Effects of Anti-Authoritarian Protest: Evidence from the West German Student Movement
articles.authors: Julian Voß
articles.abstract: How do anti-authoritarian protest movements shape electoral behavior? A recurring concern in both scholarly and public debates is that mobilization against democratic erosion and illiberal political actors may alienate moderates and generate electoral backlash. I examine this question by studying the electoral consequences of the West German student movement of the 1960s, a wave of leftist anti-authoritarian protest directed mainly against the German right. I combine city-level election results, protest event data, and a geo-located pre-election survey. Using a difference-in-differences design, I first show that exposure to protest did not generate electoral backlash at the city level. Instead, protest is associated with a differential increase in support for the center left. Individual-level survey evidence replicates these patterns and suggests that the observed shifts are driven primarily by voters defecting from the center right to the Social Democrats. Additional individual-level analyses provide evidence most consistent with framing effects: protest exposure is associated with a heightened perception of the far-right NPD as an extremist actor and with the belief that the center left was better able to curb political extremism. These findings suggest that anti-authoritarian protest can influence electoral behavior by shaping perceptions of democratic threats and underscore the potential of contentious movements to strengthen pro-democratic forces.

articles.title: Recognition Denied, Dignity Constructed: How Vocational Students Navigate Symbolic Devaluation and Construct Self-worth
articles.authors: Loïs Schenk
articles.abstract: Being seen, valued, and respected matters, yet for students in vocational education and training (VET), recognition is far from guaranteed. Drawing on Honneth's recognition theory and Lamont and colleagues' sociocultural framework, this study explores how VET students in the Netherlands experience recognition and how they draw on cultural repertoires to construct a sense of self-worth in a context that often denies it. Based on qualitative interviews with 32 VET students (Mage = 19.5, 59.38% female), the findings reveal a consistent asymmetry across Honneth's three spheres of recognition. While students report meaningful recognition in close relationships, they encounter a marked deficit at the institutional and societal level, where a shared cultural script positions academic education as superior to vocational training. In navigating this gap, students both internalise and contest a dominant cultural logic that positions academic education as superior, while mobilising three cultural repertoires to construct alternative bases for dignity and worth: passion and authenticity, practical knowledge as value, and supported self-reliance. These repertoires are best understood as responses to misrecognition rather than resolutions of it. The findings point to the importance of addressing recognition through the cultural processes by which educational hierarchies are reproduced and contested by society.

articles.title: The emergence and political relevance of supranational identity in Europe, 1971–2024
articles.authors: Theresa Kuhn; Armin Seimel; John Michaelis
articles.abstract:
Collective identities shape human social behavior, yet it remains unclear whether large-scale identities emerge and persist in heterogeneous societies. The European Union, uniting diverse populations of 27 countries, provides a unique setting to study a key question across the social sciences: Does political institution building go hand-in-hand with the emergence of a common identity? Using a Bayesian latent trait model of European identity spanning 1971–2024 based on 3.7 million survey responses
across the EU-27 and United Kingdom, we reconstruct long-term identity trajectories despite fragmented data. We find that European identity has strengthened steadily across most member states and remained resilient during existential crises. Higher identity is associated with increased turnout in European Parliament elections, underlining the political relevance of European identity. Our findings show that large-scale collective identities can emerge and consolidate in diverse societies, and that such identities are linked to participation in supranational democratic institutions.

articles.title: The Architecture of Asymmetry: Directed Structural Adhesion and Elite Closure in Interaction Networks
articles.authors: Eugenia Perekhodko
articles.abstract: Although social communication, knowledge transfer, and resource exchanges are inherently asymmetric, classical network formulations of group solidarity traditionally operationalize relational architecture through symmetric, undirected topologies. This paper resolves this theoretical and methodological limitation by extending White and Harary’s concept of structural adhesion to directed graphs, introducing a formal framework based on directed edge-disjoint pathways. Positioned as a relation-centered counterpart to vertex-based structural cohesion, this framework measures a collective's robustness against channel disruption rather than actor turnover. We evaluate the empirical utility of this methodology using 28 web-based interaction networks spanning thousands of actors. The findings demonstrate that sequential partitioning through higher-order directed adhesive layers—specifically the Largest Strongly Connected Component ($LSCC$) and the Largest 2-Edge-Connected Component ($L2ECC$)—induces a progressive, monotonic densification of individual prestige and structural capital. Furthermore, topological analysis reveals that this edge-redundant structural layer systematically contracts into an elite core whose constituent nodes occupy the highest percentiles of expertise, functioning as an automated sieve for structural closure. Ultimately, this framework provides a rigorous, robust operational tool for quantifying relational reliability, tracking information retention, and locating elite structural subcultures within asymmetric social systems.

articles.title: Geospatial Insights on the EuroHPC Supercomputing Ecosystem
articles.authors: Jukka Ruohonen
articles.abstract: Supercomputers and high-performance computing in general are increasingly important in science, innovation, and development. With this importance in mind, the research note presents a few relevant geospatial insights on the European supercomputing ecosystem built around EuroHPC, a legal and funding entity created by the European Union (EU). The focus of the insights presented is on the geographic locations of the EuroHPC’s supercomputers as well as the geographic locations of scientific and other organizations having used the supercomputers. In addition, a few relevant observations are made with respect to funded science projects to which the EuroHPC ecosystem has participated.

articles.title: Stronger Quotas, Smaller Gaps? Cultural Moderation of the Relationship Between Gender Quota Strength and Gender Gaps in Voting Across Europe, 2002–2025
articles.authors: Olga Lavrinenko; Kateryna Gryniuk
articles.abstract:
